docs.title: How to read this master sheet
docs.text:
• This is a cross-sector navigation table, not an absolute ranking list that compares banks, platforms, semiconductors, and pharma on one single multiple.
  • A true Buy / Hold / Sell needs to be established in each sector page first, then prioritized here across themes.
  • Intraday moves provide only weak sentiment input and are insufficient alone to change action.

docs.title: Quadrant overview
docs.text:
• Small dots = single companies; bubble labels = sector centers.
  • X-axis = Advantage strength = (quality_moat + growth_driver) / 2
  • Y-axis = Cost controlability = (valuation_setup + risk_control) / 2
  • Higher right and upper means stronger pros and more controllable costs; lower left means a weaker current setup.
  • Note: In the all-market chart, valuation_setup is still a relative score inside each sector basket, not a cross-sector unified multiple comparison.
  • For company-level comparison, use the per-theme charts and tables below as reference.

docs.title: How to compare this group
docs.text:
• Banks, alternative asset management, and payment networks cannot be measured with the same ruler; we first review earnings quality and regulatory sensitivity, then multiples.
  • Payment networks can tolerate higher valuation when quality is high; bank “cheapness” must be interpreted together with credit and capital requirements.
  • Names with high geography and restructuring variance will not move to Buy quickly even if multiples are low.

docs.title: Quadrant overview
docs.text:
• X-axis = Advantage strength = (quality_moat + growth_driver) / 2
  • Y-axis = Cost controlability = (valuation_setup + risk_control) / 2
  • The farther to the upper right, the stronger the pros and the more controlled the costs in this group.

docs.title: Current ranking
docs.text:
1. APO — Buy — The permanent capital + private credit engine is most complete; valuation has not become distorted yet.
  2. V — Buy — Best quality and the hardest business model in this group, and although not cheap, still a long-duration top-tier in the financial basket.
  3. JPM — Hold — Most stable large-bank sample, but regulatory discount makes it more of a quality anchor than the strongest elastic buy.
  4. BAC — Hold — Valuation is cheap, but quality and earnings elasticity are still slightly behind JPM.
  5. BX — Hold — Platform breadth is strong, but volatility transmits more directly when exit and fundraising cycles turn against it.
  6. GS — Hold — Cyclical elasticity is clear, but success still depends on stronger capital-market activity.
  7. HSBC — Sell — Geography and restructuring variables are too many, so even at modest valuation risk/reward is not the best.

docs.title: How to compare this group
docs.text:
• Compare platform control, distribution power, and AI monetization pathways first, then valuation multiples; one megacap being more expensive does not automatically push it to the bottom.
  • Valuation is based mainly on a mix of forward PE + P/S, avoiding single-multiple comparisons between AMZN’s capital-heavy platform and AAPL’s mature hardware platform.
  • TSLA — Tesla remains in this basket, but as a conditional name it is first given a risk discount.

docs.title: Quadrant overview
docs.text:
• X-axis = Advantage strength = (quality_moat + growth_driver) / 2
  • Y-axis = Cost controlability = (valuation_setup + risk_control) / 2
  • The farther to the upper right, the stronger the pros and the more controlled the costs in this group.

docs.title: Current ranking
docs.text:
1. MSFT — Buy — Enterprise distribution control and the Azure AI monetization path are the clearest; despite a premium, it remains the highest-conviction core slot in the platform basket.
  2. AMZN — Buy — The AWS + ads + retail triple-engine is still working, and on a platform-basket basis this valuation is not the most constraining.
  3. GOOG — Buy — Search cash flow provides enough cushion, and Cloud AI continues to improve the growth structure, making value-for-cash balance comparatively reasonable.
  4. META — Buy — The ad engine and AI efficiency gains are both paying off, but high CapEx and regulatory pressure keep it slightly below the most stable platform spot.
  5. AAPL — Hold — Quality is exceptional, but it currently acts more like a mature platform defensive holding; the further acceleration of AI-driven device replacement still needs confirmation.
  6. TSLA — Sell — Long-dated optionality is large, but the mismatch between auto cash flow and very high valuation is still the hardest-to-manage risk in this group.

docs.title: How to compare this group
docs.text:
• First separate platform compute, manufacturing backbone, memory cycle, and edge/analog, then do relative valuation.
  • A cheap cyclical stock does not automatically win over a scarce platform; scarcity, realization certainty, and geo/geopolitical execution risk must be considered together.
  • Conditional and transition names are given risk discounts by default, and only pulled back when valuation is exceptionally strong.

docs.title: Quadrant overview
docs.text:
• X-axis = Advantage strength = (quality_moat + growth_driver) / 2
  • Y-axis = Cost controlability = (valuation_setup + risk_control) / 2
  • The farther to the upper right, the stronger the pros and the better cost control in this group.

docs.title: Current ranking
docs.text:
1. NVDA — Buy — Platform position is strongest; even if it is not cheap, it remains the hardest-to-replace core thesis in this group.
  2. TSM — Buy — Advanced manufacturing and packaging infrastructure are scarce, and current valuation can still be partly offset by a geography discount.
  3. AVGO — Hold / staged pullback-buy only — Custom XPU plus networking duration remains first-tier, but after Q2 FY2026 the provisional line stack is 420 / 450 / 480 / 525; no fresh chase.
  4. MU — Hold — HBM tailwind is clearest, but the strong cyclical nature of memory means this is a high-quality cyclical basket rather than a long-horizon best-in-class core.
  5. QCOM — Hold / no-chase — Physical AI and data-center inference optionality are stronger than the old edge-AI frame, but the current price is already in the no-chase zone and it is still not a core AI-infrastructure leader.
  6. AMD — Hold — The second-position thesis is valid, but software ecosystem scale and monetization ramp still need to be proven.
  7. TXN — Hold — Quality is solid, but AI resilience is limited; more of a base position than a front-line pick in this group.
  8. MRVL — Hold — High upside and high concentration, odds are decent but value still trails the leaders and infrastructure layer.
  9. ARM — Sell — Scarcity is strong, but current valuation already discounts too many positive outcomes early, so margin of safety is thin.
  10. INTC — Sell — Transformation upside is large, but triple execution risk across product, manufacturing, and capex remains highest in this group.
  11. SNDK — Sell — More like a NAND cycle trade than an AI core thesis; the standalone sample window is still too short.

  • QCOM: Terminal AI odds are decent and valuation is not expensive, but it remains conditional edge compute rather than a core line.

docs.title: AI Application Production and Data Lifecycle
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-14 CEST Status: canonical spine 9. It begins when a workload has been selected for production and tracks how runtime, data/evals, permissions, recovery, workflow, and domain operations generate durable revenue, margin, and cash conversion.

docs.title: Not a renamed “AI software basket”
docs.text:
This page does not group every SaaS, BPO, cloud, or security company by sector label. Each subnode must map to a production failure point, control point, and separate monetization gate:

  1. without deployment/runtime, the model cannot serve a workload reliably;
  2. without data quality/evals/HITL, output cannot remain production-grade;
  3. without permission/security/compliance, an agent cannot safely access enterprise context;
  4. without recovery/resilience, errors, attacks, or data damage cannot be rolled back;
  5. without workflow/control plane, the model cannot execute inside approvals, rules, and systems of action;
  6. without domain operations/services, last-mile work and exception handling do not close.

docs.title: Six subnodes
docs.text: Node Production control point Primary anchors Monetization gate Key disconfirmation Developer / inference runtime deployment, serving, edge delivery, developer surface, application runtime/consumption, observability DOCN (runtime), GOOG (cloud/AI platform + application consumption), NET (edge/developer delivery), DDOG (observability/security runtime); BLZE and FSLY are adjacent context AI workload usage/revenue, application consumption, delivery/security attach, telemetry ingestion, unit economics, retention, capex/FCF generic cloud/application/traffic/telemetry growth is mislabeled AI runtime monetization Data creation / quality / evals / HITL training/post-training/evals/safety/deployment support and human fallback INOD, TASK named engagement, AI revenue/mix, margin, cash, concentration, repeatability one-off projects/pilots or low-quality labor revenue are labeled a durable control point Data/context permission / security / compliance enterprise context discovery, access policy, DSPM, endpoint/cloud/identity security, audit, fail-closed guardrail VRNS (data permission/DSPM), CRWD (endpoint/cloud/identity security); SNOW, CRM, and NOW are adjacent platform/control links SaaS ARR/adoption, protected data/users, module attach, retention, margin, security outcome AI/security language lacks product adoption, access-control, or workload-protection proof Recovery / resilience / rollback backup, cyber recovery, data/model/workflow rollback, clean-room restore CVLT, RBRK ARR/revenue, recovery adoption, retention, margin, FCF, incident-driven durability generic backup demand is labeled AI-specific monetization Workflow / BPM / system-of-action control plane rules, cases, approval, orchestration, operational deployment, audit, action execution PEGA (BPM/workflow), PLTR (enterprise/government operational deployment); CRM and NOW are registered product benchmarks, while MSFT is a demand-primary / E9-secondary distribution benchmark; ESTC and TEAM are plain-text source-back candidates only and own no active entity route AI/workflow/deployment adoption, ACV/ARR/revenue, attach, repeatability, retention, margin, cash a copilot feature or a few projects are labeled durable control-plane ownership; seat/concentration pressure is ignored Domain operations / implementation / services vertical data-decision workflow, production engineering, process operations, human exception handling GDYN, EXLS, G; TASK may secondary-link AI revenue mix, named clients/wins, project-to-run conversion, margin, utilization, concentration, cash services headlines are treated as product-like recurring moats; labor intensity and project risk are ignored

docs.title: Causal flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    W["Workload chosen for production"]
    R["Runtime / deployment"]
    D["Data / evals / HITL"]
    P["Permission / security / compliance"]
    C["Workflow / control plane"]
    O["Domain operations / services"]
    X["Recovery / rollback"]
    V["Business outcome / cash conversion"]

    W --> R --> D --> P --> C --> O --> V
    X --> R
    X --> D
    X --> C

This is not a one-way vendor stack. One production workflow repeatedly passes through observability, permission, evaluation, human exceptions, and recovery. Unique primary routing is: GOOG/DOCN/DDOG/NET to runtime/application-consumption/delivery/observability, CRWD to permission/security/compliance, and PLTR to workflow/operational deployment. MSFT remains demand-primary and appears here only as a workflow-distribution secondary benchmark. Secondary links do not create a second ownership claim. Research must prove which failure point a company controls and how that control is monetized.

docs.title: Boundaries with other spines
docs.text:
• Spine 1 Cloud and Compute Demand primary-owns payer/workload/capacity ownership. This page starts with production runtime and application monetization.
  • Spine 3 Memory, Storage, and In-System Data Movement primary-owns HBM/DRAM/CXL/flash/capacity storage. SNOW/CRM/NOW/VRNS/CVLT enterprise data/context/control economics belong here.
  • Platform Technology, Internet, and Distribution primary-owns traffic, cloud/platform distribution, consumer/commerce ecosystems, and platform cashflow. This page owns only the production control point.
  • Product/runtime control layers and services implementation must remain separate: DOCN/GOOG/DDOG/NET/CRWD/PEGA/PLTR/MSFT/CRM/NOW/VRNS/CVLT use recurring-product, usage, attach, consumption, and deployment economics; GDYN/EXLS/G/TASK use project/run-services, utilization, labor, and concentration economics.

docs.title: Evidence ladder
docs.text:
• Proven: issuer-primary adoption/ARR/revenue/AI mix, named customer/engagement, retention, margin, cash, or production outcome.
  • Issuer claim: AI product launch, agent roadmap, TAM, pipeline, partner/ecosystem wording.
  • Reasonable inference: continuously running agent workflows increase demand for evals, permission, recovery, orchestration, and human exceptions; attach, share, economics, and repeatability still need proof.
  • Not proven: an AI feature is a control point; a pilot is scaled deployment; services AI revenue has software margins; enterprise data growth is a physical storage shortage.

docs.title: Promotion / action boundary
docs.text:
• This page changes no formal discovery state and creates no Phase 7 research-seed entity. Promotion still follows issuer/valuation/risk/ownership/non-duplicate-SOT gates in Methods and Sources.
  • dated mechanism/ranking evidence: Phase 3 2026-06-06 checkpoint; not current action.
  • All E9 action clusters, including GOOG, DDOG/NET, CRWD, and PLTR, use only the sole pointer in Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger; this concept does not link directly to an action page. MSFT's demand-primary / E9-secondary route is also listed separately in that registry.
  • company dated action: use only the sole cluster pointer in Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger; if it is none, add fresh issuer/raw evidence and a market snapshot first. This page does not maintain price bands, sizing, or TradingView hlines.

docs.title: Cloud and Compute Demand

docs.title: What this spine answers
docs.text: AI infrastructure demand does not come from one buyer. Training, post-training, inference, and persistent agent workflows create workload, which becomes chip, network, facility, and power orders through different capacity models. This page owns demand and capacity economics; Semiconductors and Foundational Compute owns compute architecture, while Memory, Storage, and In-System Data Movement owns physical memory and storage.

docs.title: Five demand and ownership models
docs.text: Model Who pays / carries risk Validate first Does not automatically prove Hyperscaler-owned Large cloud/platform company owns capex and depreciation cloud usage, RPO, capacity capex, utilization, FCF a supplier's share or margin AI-native / model lab Model company buys, reserves, or partner-finances capacity usage/revenue, long-term commitment, concentration, unit economics headline capacity equals durable profit Neo-cloud Specialist GPU cloud owns or finances equipment contracted capacity, utilization, debt/lease, GPU residual value all backlog is high-quality take-or-pay Colocation / leased capacity Colo/REIT or tenant leases site and power lease term, pre-lease, power delivery, tenant concentration a signed lease equals energized capacity Enterprise-private / sovereign Enterprise or government deploys in owned/hosted environments production workload, budget owner, security/data residency, cadence pilot or sovereign headline equals broad commercial demand

docs.title: Existing demand anchors and routes
docs.text:
• ORCL: OCI/RPO/capacity expansion is one of the clearest local demand anchors. Action uses only the sole cluster pointer in Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger; if it is none, refresh sources first.
  • MSFT, AMZN, GOOG, and META: large platform/hyperscaler benchmarks; separate consumer/advertising businesses from capacity economics.
  • The internal Anthropic/SpaceX evidence line preserves only the verified narrow compute-capacity tie; it does not extend to generic suppliers, SpaceX operations, or IPO beneficiaries.
  • Platform Technology, Internet, and Distribution: portfolio lens for large platforms and consumer/internet business models; it no longer owns capacity-economics SOT.

docs.title: Validation metrics
docs.text:
• workload: training/post-training/inference mix, token/agent usage, production deployment;
  • contracts: RPO, take-or-pay, lease term, concentration, cancellation and financing terms;
  • economics: utilization, usage revenue, gross margin, depreciation, capex intensity, FCF;
  • delivery: land, utility interconnect, energized MW, network readiness, rack-deployment cadence;
  • disconfirming evidence: capacity outruns usage, circular financing, worsening GPU depreciation/residual value, customer cancellation, power delay, or persistent FCF mismatch.

docs.title: Ownership boundaries
docs.text:
• Spine 1 owns workload, payer, capacity owner, and economics.
  • Compute platforms/custom silicon belong to Semiconductors and Foundational Compute.
  • HBM/DRAM/flash/interface/CXL belong to Memory, Storage, and In-System Data Movement.
  • Enterprise data/workflow/permission control planes and production runtime belong to AI Application Production and Data Lifecycle.
  • This page does not maintain buy/sell/price bands; Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger points each ticker/cluster to one current action SOT.

docs.title: Data Center Buildout Home
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 CEST Status: master router for the coupled AI/data-center system. It explains causal ownership and reading order; it does not maintain candidate rankings, price actions, or supplier share.

docs.title: Not one ticker supply chain
docs.text:
AI workload, compute, memory, networking, semiconductor realization, systems manufacturing, power delivery, facility delivery, and application productionization converge in parallel and feed back into each other. They are not a one-way demand → chip → network → manufacturing → facility assembly line.

Closed-loop reading:

production usage/outcome → workload and capacity budget → compute/memory/network + manufacturing + site delivery → energized capacity → production usage/outcome

Time-to-revenue is set by the slowest, scarcest, and least substitutable parallel node.

docs.title: Nine primary spines
docs.text:
Spine Canonical ownership First-read page Main boundary 1. Demand / capacity ownership workload, payer, owned/leased/financed capacity, utilization/revenue/FCF Cloud and Compute Demand demand does not prove supplier share 2. Compute platforms & custom silicon GPU/accelerator, custom ASIC/XPU, CPU/host, architecture/IP/EDA Semiconductors and Foundational Compute excludes foundry/package realization 3. Memory / storage / in-system data movement HBM, DRAM, interface/controller/CXL, flash, capacity storage Memory, Storage, and In-System Data Movement excludes enterprise data/workflow software 4. Networking / optical / DCI fabric, scale-up/out, AEC/copper, optical, DCI/coherent AI Interconnect, Optical Networking, and DCI power components and EMS manufacturing are separate 5. Semiconductor manufacturing / AP / test / materials foundry, HBM/package, substrate, bonding, inspection, probe/test/KGD, materials Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials compute architecture and rack manufacturing are separate 6. Systems / racks / complex manufacturing server/rack, EMS/NPI, network/optical manufacturing, working capital/margin Systems, Racks, and Complex Manufacturing DELL/CLS/SANM/FN leave packaging/optical primary ownership 7. Generation / grid / time-to-power generation/fuel, grid/interconnect, onsite bridge, storage/backup, project timing Power Generation, Grid, and Fuel Supply · Onsite Bridge Power, Storage, and Backup ends at utility/site boundary 8. Facility / rack power / cooling / delivery site entry, transformer/switchgear/protection, rack/board power, cooling, controls, EPC/MEP Facility Electrical, Rack Power, Cooling, and Delivery site boundary to energized rack 9. AI application production / data lifecycle developer runtime, data/evals/HITL, permission/security, workflow, recovery, domain operations/services AI Application Production and Data Lifecycle separate from spine 1 payer/capacity, spine 3 physical storage, and platform-distribution economics

Cross-theme finance, healthcare, space, and China-platform research continues through Cross-Sector Watchlist Home rather than the AI main chain.

B/C/D/E/F/G/H generally advance in parallel. Arrows show major dependencies, not the only sequence or automatic revenue attribution.

docs.title: Demand / capacity
docs.text: Cloud and Compute Demand is no longer an ORCL ticker list. It separates hyperscaler, AI-native/model-lab, neo-cloud, colo/lease, and enterprise-private/sovereign capacity while putting utilization, depreciation, financing, and FCF back into the demand test.

docs.title: Compute architecture
docs.text: Semiconductors and Foundational Compute primary-owns GPU/custom silicon/CPU/IP/EDA/system architecture only. TSM foundry/package realization and MU/SNDK/WDC/RMBS physical memory/storage economics now route to spines 5 and 3.

docs.title: Physical memory and storage
docs.text: Memory, Storage, and In-System Data Movement separates HBM, host memory, interface/controller/CXL, datacenter flash, and capacity storage. It does not treat storage financial realization as HBM physics scarcity or place SNOW/CRM/NOW/DOCN in the physical spine.

docs.title: Networking / optical / DCI
docs.text: AI Interconnect, Optical Networking, and DCI primary-owns networking/fabric platforms, interconnect semis, optical engines/modules, and DCI/coherent transport only. FN/SANM/CLS/Jabil NPI/EMS/test economics route to spine 6; NVTS/AEIS/VICR/BELFB power economics route to spine 8.

docs.title: Semiconductor realization and systems manufacturing
docs.text: Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials primary-owns wafer/foundry, package/bonding, inspection/metrology, probe/test/KGD, AP&T data, and substrate/materials. Systems, Racks, and Complex Manufacturing primary-owns DELL/CLS/SANM/FN server/rack, EMS/NPI, optical/network manufacturing, working-capital, and margin economics. Their boundary is qualified package → deployable system.

docs.title: Power line 7/8 boundary
docs.text: Power Generation, Grid, and Fuel Supply and Onsite Bridge Power, Storage, and Backup jointly form spine 7, primary-owning generation/grid/interconnection and bridge/resilience respectively; both end at the utility/site boundary. Facility Electrical, Rack Power, Cooling, and Delivery starts after that boundary and primary-owns the existing ETN/POWL/HPS.A, AEIS/BELFB/NVTS/VICR, VRT/JCI/NVT, and PWR/EME boundary-to-rack routes. ASTK was retired from active ownership in Phase 3 R1a. BLDP and PLUG retain stable entity paths but route through the onsite hub only as hydrogen-bridge context: BLDP is a pilot-validation benchmark and PLUG is special-situation optionality; neither enters the near-term primary power ranking.

docs.title: Research routing
docs.text:
• structural mechanism: start here, then use the canonical concept hub;
  • proof gap / peer economics: use the relevant ledger, evidence map, or comparison;
  • company mechanism: use the entity page; one company has one SOT and may receive secondary links from several spines;
  • dated action: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger points each ticker/cluster to one current-live SOT;
  • primary evidence: return to frontmatter sources: raw captures or packets.

docs.title: Sector background
docs.text:
• IEA: global data-center electricity use was about 415 TWh in 2024 and approaches 945 TWh in the 2030 baseline. Scale makes site/power constraints important but does not replace company evidence.
  • DOE/LBNL: U.S. data-center electricity use was about 176 TWh in 2023 and may rise to 325–580 TWh by 2028. The range itself shows high delivery-timing and scenario uncertainty.

docs.title: What this spine answers
docs.text: After power reaches the campus boundary, transformers, switchgear, bus/protection, power rooms, rack/board conversion, cooling, controls, commissioning, and EPC/MEP must still turn it into stable compute. This page owns boundary-to-rack economics. It does not own generation/grid/interconnection or onsite-bridge economics.

docs.title: 800V / rack-power boundary
docs.text:
• NVTS/VICR primary roles are board-side/HVDC/near-load conversion architecture; AEIS/BELFB are closer to rack-entry PSU/power-shelf/protection/magnetics. All four belong to spine 8 but do not share one economic model.
  • NVIDIA/ecosystem/architecture wording is an Issuer claim or named-ecosystem evidence. Only program/order/revenue/margin upgrades company monetization proof.
  • GEV/HUBB have their primary parent in spine 7 generation/grid/interconnection. Facility products may receive a secondary link without duplicate primary ownership here.

docs.title: Evidence ladder
docs.text:
• Proven: data-center orders/backlog/revenue, a named program/deployment, shipment/commissioning, margin, or cash evidence.
  • Issuer claim: guidance/outlook, product architecture, ecosystem qualification, pipeline, TAM, or future capacity.
  • Reasonable inference: higher rack density/800V/liquid cooling raises electrical/thermal content; attach, share, project timing, and margin still need proof.
  • Not proven: entry into an 800V ecosystem is procurement; power scarcity benefits every electrical name; facility backlog is an energized rack or FCF.

docs.title: Primary ownership and outbound routing
docs.text:
• This page primary-owns the ETN/POWL/HPS.A, AEIS/BELFB/NVTS/VICR, VRT/JCI/NVT, and PWR/EME boundary-to-rack routes. ASTK and STEM are retired and retain stable-path historical provenance only; neither owns a current route.
  • GEV/HUBB and generation-asset/fuel/grid/interconnection economics belong to Power Generation, Grid, and Fuel Supply.
  • BE/PSIX/GNRC/CAT/FLNC/BLDP/PLUG bridge/resilience belongs to Onsite Bridge Power, Storage, and Backup.
  • DELL/CLS/SANM/FN system-side rack integration belongs to Systems, Racks, and Complex Manufacturing. This page owns the site electrical/thermal/commissioning interface only.

docs.title: Why this layer merits separate tracking
docs.text:
• These assets determine how borrowing costs and capital-market activity transmit into valuation.
  • Banks, investment firms, and alternative asset managers have very different earnings cycles, so they cannot be mixed.
  • For the cross-sector watchlist, they mostly play the role of discount-rate and risk-appetite transmission.

docs.title: Large integrated banks
docs.text:
• JPM: The thickest balance sheet and highest quality, but valuation remains hard to escape regulatory discounting.
  • BAC: Deposit and wealth-management franchise is strong; watch credit and rate sensitivity closely.
  • HSBC: Asia cross-border network advantage, but geostrategic and restructuring risks are highest.

docs.title: Investment banking and trading
docs.text: • GS: One of the purest names in investment-banking execution; high cyclical beta and high volatility.

docs.title: Alternative asset management / private credit
docs.text:
• BX: Breadth remains the main strength and private-market beta is high, but fundraising and redemption cycles can reverse quickly.
  • APO: Athene provides a permanent-capital amplifier; model is strong, but credit and regulatory complexity is higher.

docs.title: Payment infrastructure
docs.text: • V: Global consumption flow toll collection power; business is strong, but regulation is always close.

docs.title: Core lines I prefer to track now
docs.text:
• In macro uncertainty, JPM and V are better quality observation points.
  • When risk appetite increases, GS, BX, and APO show stronger cyclical beta.
  • HSBC remains a special case with geopolitical and region-specific positioning.

docs.title: Main risk focus
docs.text:
• Regulation and capital requirements can instantly reframe valuation caps for large financial names.
  • Alternative managers look strong in benign credit conditions, but fundraising, redemption, and credit events can compress value and payouts quickly.
  • Payment networks are stable but not immune to regulatory pressure, fee litigation, and large-customer bargaining.

docs.title: Why this layer merits separate tracking
docs.text:
• These names look “platform-like” at first glance, but in substance this is credit, capital supply, and regulation-driven business.
  • Their volatility often exceeds traditional finance because the market prices growth, tech narratives, and credit quality simultaneously.
  • In the cross-sector lens, they amplify risk appetite and the consumer credit cycle.

docs.title: Digital banking / super apps
docs.text: • SOFI: The most expansive platform-style narrative; user growth, credit quality, and acquisition efficiency determine upside limits.

docs.title: BNPL and flexible payments
docs.text:
• KLAR: One of the strongest mental brands in Europe, but credit, regulation, and competition are heavy.
  • AFRM: Strong merchant distribution and simple core product; funding cost and credit performance remain anchors.

docs.title: AI credit infrastructure
docs.text:
• PGY: More B2B credit infrastructure than consumer-facing; leverage can be meaningful when capital markets stay supportive.
  • UPST: The AI narrative is back, but capital supply and delinquency remain decisive.

docs.title: Retail transaction entry
docs.text: • HOOD: Strong user entry and fast perimeter expansion; transaction volume and regulation can amplify volatility.

docs.title: Main lines I prefer to track now
docs.text:
• For platform expansion in financialization, SOFI and HOOD are more user-entry style names.
  • For credit technology exposure, PGY and UPST are high-beta, high-volatility names.
  • For payments and installment cognition, KLAR and AFRM are closest to direct consumer competition.

docs.title: Main risk focus
docs.text:
• The biggest risk is sudden funding tightening, where many models reveal fragility when liquidity support disappears.
  • Credit quality and regulatory interpretation can quickly change valuation frameworks.
  • Many names are still framed as “platforms,” but the core business remains credit and distribution efficiency.

docs.title: AI Interconnect, Optical Networking, and DCI
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 CEST Status: canonical spine 4. It primary-owns networking/fabric, interconnect semiconductors, optical engines/modules, and DCI/coherent transport. The stable legacy path Interconnect, Optics, and Power Components.md remains only for link compatibility; it no longer implies power-component ownership.

docs.title: What this spine answers
docs.text: AI-cluster value is not set by one accelerator. In-node scale-up, node-to-node scale-out, rack/cluster fabric, scale-across/DCI, and copper/optical signal integrity jointly determine effective bandwidth, latency, utilization, and scalability. This page owns those transport and networking mechanisms. It does not attribute contract manufacturing, test yield, or power-component revenue to networking.

docs.title: Four subnodes
docs.text: Node Problem solved Current local anchors Key disconfirmation Networking / fabric platform switching/routing, fabric OS, cluster/DCI control, and integrated optical transport ANET benchmark; NOK; CSCO/CIEN external benchmarks AI orders fail to become revenue/margin, or merchant/custom fabric loses share Interconnect semis / signal integrity AEC/ACC, retimer/CDR/equalizer, DSP/TIA, fabric switch, PCIe/CXL/UALink, and copper/optical signal chain CRDO, ALAB benchmark, MRVL, SMTC, MXL named customer/revenue/backlog remains open, or standards/architecture substitute Optical engine / module / component lasers, transceivers, silicon photonics, CPO/NPO, fiber/connectivity, and InP substrate COHR, LITE, MTSI, AAOI, GLW, AXTI capacity leads demand, pricing erodes, customer concentration or materials/export constraint DCI / coherent / open optical transport 800G/coherent transport and open optical networking across clusters, campuses, and regions NOK, CIEN benchmark, ADTN, optical-platform anchors generic telecom recovery is misread as AI/DCI revenue

docs.title: Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 CEST Status: canonical spine 5. The stable legacy path Manufacturing, Packaging, and Systems Integration.md remains for link compatibility; this page no longer primary-owns server/rack, EMS/NPI, or optical-manufacturing economics.

docs.title: What this spine answers
docs.text: Spine 2 compute architecture defines what chips are needed and spine 3 defines the physical memory/storage layer. This page explains how die, HBM stacks, substrates, and materials are mass-produced, bonded, inspected, tested, and turned into qualified semiconductor packages. Value capture comes from capacity, yield, process control, qualification, and known-good-die—not final server/rack assembly.

docs.title: Six subnodes
docs.text: Node Problem solved Current local anchors Key disconfirmation Foundry / wafer / package platform leading-edge wafer, CoWoS/SoIC, wafer/package capacity, and integration TSM, ASX, AMKR capex/capacity fails to become shipment, utilization, yield, or margin Bonding / attach / debond temporary bond/debond, TCB, hybrid/D2W bonding, and thin-wafer handling BESI benchmark, SMHN qualification/ramp slips or orders fail to become revenue Inspection / metrology finds defects, measures critical dimensions, controls chiplet/HBM package process windows ONTO, CAMT AI/AP exposure cannot be separated from the broader wafer cycle Probe / test / KGD screens good die and validates HBM/chiplet/packages before and after expensive assembly FORM, TER HBM/chiplet complexity fails to raise content, utilization, or mix AP&T process-control data connects fab/test/assembly data and yield analytics PDFS software/data claims do not become AP&T/OSAT adoption or revenue Substrate / materials / purity ABF/FC-BGA, glass/package substrate, chemicals/gases, and process support AT&S, MKSI, ENTG, 3037 research routes; GLW secondary link generic semiconductor/material exposure is misread as AI/AP monetization

docs.title: Concept-line map: choose the spine before evidence and action
docs.text:
This page now routes by problem chain, not by the newest data pile. Reading order: 1. choose the relevant spine; 2. read the concept hub to understand the bottleneck layer; 3. use the tracking ledger or current-live page for proof gaps and action discipline; 4. verify claims back to entity pages and local raw / research-packet sources.

Spine What it answers First-read pages Currentness / ownership boundary 1. AI demand / capacity ownership / workload economics Who creates workload, pays for capacity, and turns owned/leased/financed capacity into utilization, revenue, and FCF. Cloud and Compute Demand · Data Center Buildout Home Demand proof does not prove supplier share. 2. Compute platforms & custom silicon How GPUs/accelerators, custom ASICs/XPUs, CPU/host compute, and architecture/IP/EDA execute workload. Semiconductors and Foundational Compute · custom-ASIC dated relative-value evidence Architecture ownership excludes foundry/package realization; action still enters through the unified ticker ledger. 3. Physical memory / storage / in-system data movement How HBM, DRAM, interface/controller/CXL, datacenter flash, and capacity storage feed compute systems. Memory, Storage, and In-System Data Movement · Storage, Memory, and CPU-Adjacent Bottleneck Follow-up Tracking Ledger Physical storage is not enterprise data/workflow software; storage realization is not HBM scarcity. 4. AI networking / optical / DCI How fabric, DCI, DSP, AEC/copper, and optical engines connect nodes, clusters, and sites. AI Interconnect, Optical Networking, and DCI · AI Optical Interconnect and DCI Hidden Treasure Monitoring Metrics Ledger Networking/optical stays separate from power components and EMS manufacturing. 5. Semiconductor manufacturing / AP / test / materials How foundry, HBM/package, substrate, bonding, inspection, probe/test, and KGD realize architecture. Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials · Advanced Packaging and HBM Bottleneck Evidence Closure Table Evidence maps do not become action sheets; systems/rack manufacturing is separate. 6. Systems / racks / complex manufacturing Server/rack architecture, EMS/NPI, network/optical manufacturing, and working-capital/margin economics. Systems, Racks, and Complex Manufacturing DELL/CLS/SANM/FN have one primary parent. 7. Generation / grid / bridge / time-to-power How fuel/generation assets, grid/interconnection, onsite bridge, storage/backup, and project timing deliver power to the utility/site boundary. Power Generation, Grid, and Fuel Supply · Onsite Bridge Power, Storage, and Backup Ownership ends at the boundary handoff. 8. Facility / rack power / cooling / delivery How site-entry electrical, transformers/switchgear/protection, rack/board power, cooling, controls, and EPC/MEP create an energized rack. Facility Electrical, Rack Power, Cooling, and Delivery Starts after the boundary; GEV/HUBB and onsite bridge are not duplicate primary owners. 9. AI application production / data lifecycle Which developer runtime, data/evals/HITL, permission/security, workflow, recovery, and domain operations/services control production failure points and monetize them. AI Application Production and Data Lifecycle · 2026-06-06 evidence/ranking checkpoint Separate product control layers from services economics; not a platform-incumbent basket. Cross-theme / non-tech / portfolio lens Finance, fintech, healthcare, China platforms, event-driven, and space/satellite themes outside one AI main chain. Cross-Sector Watchlist Home · Cross-Sector Watchlist Master Scorecard Portfolio/theme lens, not an AI data-center chain.

docs.title: Memory, Storage, and In-System Data Movement
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 CEST Status: canonical spine for physical AI memory and storage. It excludes enterprise data clouds, data governance, and workflow software.

docs.title: Why this is a separate spine
docs.text: Compute is more than the accelerator. Model weights, KV cache, training data, checkpoints, and production data move among HBM, host memory, flash/storage, and interface/controller layers. Their physical capacity, bandwidth, latency, endurance, and supply cycles are different economic problems from compute architecture in Semiconductors and Foundational Compute, package/yield realization in Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials, and the data-control layer of AI productionization.

docs.title: Five subnodes
docs.text: Node Problem solved Main economic variables Current local anchors HBM / accelerator memory feeds high-bandwidth data to accelerators stack capacity, bit growth, pricing, qualification, yield MU; Samsung/SK hynix as sector benchmarks DRAM / host memory supports CPU hosts, inference, and large-memory working sets server mix, capacity, cycle, power/latency MU Interface / controller / CXL connects memory, accelerator, CPU, and pooled expansion attach, standard adoption, IP royalty, controller content RMBS Datacenter flash low-latency persistence, checkpoints, retrieval, and hot/warm tiers enterprise mix, contract quality, pricing, JV/capex SNDK, WDC Capacity storage / hierarchy retains data at scale and tiers cost exabyte growth, nearline mix, TCO, utilization WDC; adjacent cloud storage has separate service economics

docs.title: Physical transmission map
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Accelerator / CPU workload"]
    H["HBM / DRAM"]
    I["Interface · controller · CXL"]
    F["Datacenter flash"]
    C["Capacity storage"]
    D["Production data / checkpoint / retrieval"]

    D --> C
    C --> F
    F --> I
    I --> H
    H --> A
    A --> D

This is a cyclical data hierarchy, not a one-way HBM → flash → disk replacement chain. Workload mix determines each layer's capacity, bandwidth, latency, and cost weight.

docs.title: Evidence ladder
docs.text:
• Proven: company disclosure connects AI/datacenter demand to realized revenue, shipment, contract, or segment economics.
  • Issuer claim: guidance/outlook, roadmap, capability, qualification, or TAM language without company-level dollars.
  • Reasonable inference: workload growth increases memory/storage intensity; mix, pricing, and margin must still validate value capture.
  • Not proven: all storage is scarce like HBM; enterprise data software and physical storage share one valuation/bottleneck framework.

docs.title: Boundary rules
docs.text:
• Accelerator/custom silicon/CPU/IP/EDA primary ownership belongs to Semiconductors and Foundational Compute.
  • HBM package integration, bonding, substrate, inspection, probe/test, and KGD manufacturing ownership belongs to Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials.
  • SNOW, CRM, NOW, DOCN, and similar enterprise data/cloud/workflow economics belong to AI Application Production and Data Lifecycle, not this physical spine.
  • One company may be cross-linked, but company SOT remains in one entity page.

docs.text: This page is not for a single chain or one theme cluster; it is the methods page for the full unified research system. It merges the old chain-research workflow of "confirm chain position, then industry calibration, then compress the judgment" with the cross-theme watchlist workflow of "bucket first, then compare by a unified scoring discipline."

docs.title: Shared discipline
docs.text:
1. First confirm which chain or bucket a company/page belongs to, rather than chasing short-term price moves.
  2. Prioritize primary disclosures, official product pages, annual reports/quarterly filings, and official press releases.
  3. Industry-level theses only calibrate; they do not replace company-level evidence.
  4. Final outputs should be compressed into reusable judgments, not narrative stacks.
  5. Separate bottleneck position / business quality / valuation state; importance is not the same as undervaluation.

docs.title: Beta entity research-writing contract
docs.text:
Every materially revised entity page answers the same questions in this order:

  1. How the company makes money: explain products, customers, and business model in plain language rather than starting with a ticker list.
  2. Primary lane: assign one canonical causal lane; use secondary links for adjacent exposure instead of duplicating ownership.
  3. How AI demand becomes operating results: show the path to revenue, margin, and cash flow, or state clearly that the path is not yet proven.
  4. Evidence ladder: classify key claims as Proven, Issuer claim, Reasonable inference, or Not proven; product capability is not company-level monetization.
  5. Risks and kill criteria: use company-specific falsifiers, not a generic risk list.
  6. Separate structural role from discovery state: page status describes browse/navigation role; formal discovery state and workflow modifier remain separate.
  7. Action SOT: an entity's sole action entry is Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger. That registry selects the current-live SOT for the relevant subspine / action cluster, or explicitly records none. Entity pages may link mechanism/evidence pages, but must not present them as a second action authority or copy dated price bands, sizing, or buy/sell triggers.

docs.title: Formal discovery taxonomy (mutually exclusive)
docs.text:
At one as-of point, a name has at most one formal state:

  • Hidden: issuer-primary evidence shows quantifiable monetization; current market, valuation, and risk gates all pass; the critical node remains outside mainstream framing.
  • Half-hidden: all gates also pass; the market knows the AI exposure but still uses the wrong legacy label, purity assumption, or earnings sensitivity.
  • Market-found: the mechanism may be real, but price or coverage has substantially recognized it; prior discovery gap is only workflow modifier=former-half-hidden.
  • Bridge / Benchmark: explains architecture, cycle, or peer economics without claiming a discovery gap.
  • Research seed: mechanism and at least one primary route exist, but monetization, valuation, or risk gates remain open.
  • Needs-source: only capability, TAM, ecosystem, or indirect mapping exists; company-level evidence is insufficient.
  • Reject / Retire: should not remain in the active AI tree because of delisting, absent current monetization, structural duplication, or thesis invalidation.

former-half-hidden, re-underwrite, proof-first, no-chase, pilot-validation, and special-situation are workflow modifiers only; they never form a second formal state.

docs.title: Promotion gates
docs.text: Promotion from seed/needs-source requires issuer-primary monetization, a dated market/valuation screen, capital-structure and risk review, canonical ownership, and a non-duplicate SOT. For a new candidate in this workflow, any open gate means: do not create an entity page, assign status: core|active, add it to candidate/current-action navigation, upgrade it to hidden, or generate a watchlist/buy action. An existing page that is independently justified by repeated references may remain status: context, but that does not pass the promotion gate.

docs.title: Source layers
docs.text:
• HERMES current authority: docs/ops/markets/tradingview/generated/HERMES/HERMES.latest-state.md + HERMES.sectioned.json; historical target/readback JSON remains an evidence trail only.
  • Frozen TradingView watchlist / normalized manifest: the 2026-04-16 historical watchlist snapshot layer, not the current HERMES/TradingView watchlist authority.
  • Raw market snapshots: internal market snapshot layer
  • Official IR / annual report / quarterly results / product pages: private primary-document layer
  • Chain-level calibration: IEA, DOE/LBNL, Berkeley Lab, technical media, and others

docs.title: Extra rules for chain-research lens
docs.text:
• Confirm chain position first, then define bull case / risk / one-line judgment.
  • Ask three questions:
  • Who truly resolves the bottlenecks of data-center expansion;
  • Who is just being mapped into the theme;
  • Who has such a long monetization chain that extra risk discount is needed.
  • Classification thresholds:
  • direct: product/service is itself the core bottleneck in data-center expansion.
  • conditional: logic is valid, but monetization strength depends on projects, cadence, or end-user structure.
  • edge: theme-related but mostly mapping, pilot, or non-core revenue.

Five scoring dimensions
docs.text:
• quality_moat
  • growth_driver

docs.title: Industry valuation framework
docs.text:
• Platform tech / semis: prioritize forward PE, and use P/S if needed.
  • Financial institutions / capital markets: check earnings quality and regulatory sensitivity first, then PE.
  • Fintech / consumer credit: prioritize P/S, earnings pathway, and source of capital.
  • Pharma / biotech: combine PE, pipeline, patent cliffs, and policy risk.

docs.title: Comparison labels (not current-action authority)
docs.text:
• Buy: the most attractive relative risk/reward tier in the comparison schema.
  • Hold: still worth monitoring, but odds, risks, or valuation are not strong enough for the top tier.
  • Sell: the weakest relative setup in the comparison schema, or a story too far ahead of execution.
  • These legacy labels are relative ranking only; they do not authorize execution, price bands, sizing, or hlines. Current wiki action still routes only through the unified ticker ledger.

docs.title: As-of and maintenance discipline
docs.text:
• Comparison pages refresh the internal market snapshot layer first, then update relative labels, evidence, and total scores; they do not directly update current action. Action changes must follow the writeback discipline below by updating the unified ticker ledger and its sole current-live SOT.
  • Raw captures are immutable.
  • Every durable update must keep index.md and log.md in sync.
  • Temporary watchlist names should not be treated as durable structure.
  • Canvas is for navigation, not exhaustive listing; Excalidraw historical material is no longer active layer.

docs.title: Concept-line writeback discipline
docs.text:
1. New research waves create source archive root（私有研究库）source captures and packet summaries first; they do not directly rewrite concept hubs or action pages.
  2. Stable structural deltas write back to the relevant concept spine hub or tracking ledger:
  3. concept hubs explain where a line sits;
  4. follow-up ledgers preserve proof gaps, upgrade/downgrade triggers, and dated TradingView/HERMES provenance; unless the unified registry selects one as the action SOT, it cannot maintain current lines or execution boundaries;
  5. ticker ledgers collect lane/first-page routing when a name appears across multiple packets.
  6. Wiki action changes first update Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger and then the one source-backed current-live SOT selected by that registry; if the row is none, there is no current wiki action. Entity pages may update durable role/evidence/kill criteria, while scorecards and dated action compendia may preserve evidence/history, but none is a second action authority. HERMES latest-state / sectioned JSON remains the operational watchlist authority and does not create a second wiki action pointer.
  7. Selection is an explicit allowlist: any page absent from the registry's action-SOT column is historical/evidence-only regardless of a legacy current-live title or preserved tactical fields. none has no fallback through an evidence link.
  8. Historical packet pages are preserved for provenance, but index/log/router text must label them as historical checkpoints when later conclusions drift.
  9. Visual pages and canvases are browse-layer companions; they can route readers but cannot override concept-spine ownership, ledger/current-live action routing, entity durable thesis, or raw-source authority.

docs.title: Onsite Bridge Power, Storage, and Backup
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 CEST Status: bridge/resilience half of canonical spine 7. The stable path Onsite Power, Storage, and Backup Power.md remains; ownership ends at the utility/site-boundary handoff.

docs.title: What this half-spine answers
docs.text: When large power, transmission/distribution, and formal interconnection are not ready on time, how can a campus use onsite generation, microgrids, storage, or backup to shorten time-to-power and improve resilience? This page owns how power is supplemented before the handoff. It does not own post-boundary switchgear/transformers/protection, rack/board conversion, cooling, or facility delivery.

docs.title: Three subnodes
docs.text: Node Problem solved Primary anchors Key disconfirmation Onsite bridge power fuel cell, engine/generator, behind-the-meter supply, and fast deployment BE, PSIX, GNRC, CAT project/order fails to become installed MW, revenue, margin, or uptime economics Storage / campus resilience peak support, backup, microgrid flexibility, and grid/site buffering FLNC backlog/customer concentration, gross margin, or software/asset quality remains open Hydrogen / pilot backup long-duration backup and lower-carbon pilot route BLDP=pilot-validation benchmark; PLUG=special-situation optionality; both are context, not primary anchors demonstration / application wording does not become repeat deployment, quantified project economics, or sustainable cash economics

docs.title: Evidence ladder
docs.text:
• Proven: issuer disclosure gives a named project/customer, installed/contracted capacity, orders/backlog/revenue, margin, availability, or an achieved project milestone.
  • Issuer claim: guidance/outlook, pipeline, product capability, pilot, TAM, or future deployment.
  • Reasonable inference: grid delay raises onsite/backup value; economics, repeatability, permitting/fuel, and customer concentration still need proof.
  • Not proven: a pilot is scaled deployment; backlog is cash; any data-center wording proves bridge-power revenue.

docs.text:
• This page primary-owns the BE/PSIX/GNRC/CAT/FLNC bridge/resilience routes. STEM is retired from AI navigation; BLDP/PLUG retain stable paths but only as hydrogen context: BLDP=Bridge / Benchmark + pilot-validation, and PLUG=Bridge / Benchmark + special-situation.

  • ETN/POWL/HPS.A, NVTS/VICR/AEIS/BELFB, VRT/JCI/NVT, and PWR/EME boundary-to-rack economics belong to Facility Electrical, Rack Power, Cooling, and Delivery.

docs.text: Assets in pharmaceuticals, drugmakers, and biotech. The key is not “all are doing medicine,” but stability of business model, pipeline depth, patent cycle, and policy pricing pressure.

docs.title: Why this layer is worth separate focus
docs.text:
• Pharma often shows a risk-return profile very different from tech and finance in macro swings.
  • Segmentation matters: health-care services integration, mature pharma, and high-R&D biotech have different valuation frameworks.
  • In this watchlist, this layer behaves more like “cash-flow quality + pipeline + pricing power” in combination.

docs.title: Health-care services integration
docs.text: • CVS: Pharmacy + PBM + insurance integration remains scarce; merger and PBM policy risks cannot be ignored.

docs.title: Large pharma
docs.text:
• LLY: GLP-1 / GIP tailwinds remain strong, with supply, pricing, and overly high expectations as the main offset risks.
  • GSK: Vaccine + specialist-drug mix is improving; if later pipeline steps deliver, repricing room still exists.
  • MRK: Keytruda cash flow remains strong; the key issue is not now but successor throughput after the patent cliff.

docs.title: Biotech platform
docs.text: • REGN: Antibody platform strength is robust and pipeline breadth is wide, but single-product reliance and clinical swing risk are still high.

docs.title: Primary lines I track now
docs.text:
• The clearest high-growth line is LLY.
  • For stable cash flow and valuation transitions, MRK and GSK deserve more attention.
  • REGN is a high-quality platform-style biotech, but with much larger swing risk than large pharma.
  • CVS is closer to policy and utilization-driven trading, not comparable on a simple basis with pure pharma names.

docs.title: Main risk focus
docs.text:
• Drug pricing and reimbursement policy can directly rewrite valuation centers.
  • Pharma and biotech are vulnerable when short-term sales growth is mistaken for durable platform quality.
  • Health-care service integration is more exposed to operations, loss ratio, and simultaneous regulatory deterioration.

docs.text:
^b62ea1

Updated: 2026-07-13 CEST Status: upstream/grid half of canonical spine 7. The stable path Power Generation and Fuel Supply.md remains; ownership ends at the utility/site boundary and interconnection handoff.

docs.title: What this half-spine answers
docs.text: This page asks where electricity comes from, whether fuel and generation capacity are available, whether grid/transmission/distribution/interconnection can deliver it to the campus boundary, and whether permitting/queue/project timing allows on-time capacity. It does not own site-entry switchgear, rack/board power, cooling, or facility EPC/MEP after the boundary.

docs.title: Four subnodes
docs.text: Node Problem solved Primary anchors Key disconfirmation Fuel / long-duration supply nuclear fuel and long-duration available supply LEU policy, permitting, qualification, or delivery timing fails Generation / asset owner existing/new dispatchable power, contracted capacity, and asset economics VST, CEG, TLN, long-duration OKLO contract/asset availability, regulation, capex/financing, or cash conversion breaks Grid / generation equipment platform turbine/generation equipment, grid equipment, and electrification backlog GEV orders/backlog fail to become shipments, margin, service revenue, or grid capacity Utility/grid interconnect transmission/distribution hardware, utility connection, and project timing HUBB; utility-scale delivery may secondary-link PWR broad grid demand does not close to data-center/site delivery

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    F["Fuel / generation asset"]
    G["Generation + grid equipment"]
    T["Transmission / distribution / interconnect"]
    B["Utility / site boundary handoff"]
    O["Onsite bridge / resilience"]

    F --> G --> T --> B
    O --> B
    B --> S

This page primary-owns F/G/T; Onsite Bridge Power, Storage, and Backup primary-owns O. B is the shared handoff, not duplicate ownership. S belongs to spine 8 Facility Electrical, Rack Power, Cooling, and Delivery.

docs.title: Evidence ladder
docs.text:
• Proven: issuer disclosure gives assets/contracts/operating capacity, generation/grid orders/backlog, an achieved interconnection/project milestone, margin, or cash evidence.
  • Issuer claim: guidance/outlook, pipeline, future capacity, TAM, partnership, or permitting/queue expectation.
  • Reasonable inference: data-center load growth raises generation/grid demand; company assets/orders and timing still need proof.
  • Not proven: power scarcity automatically attributes to every utility/equipment name; headline MW equals near-term energization; grid backlog equals a site-ready rack.

docs.title: Primary ownership and outbound routing
docs.text:
• This spine-7 page primary-owns LEU/OKLO/TLN/VST/CEG/GEV/HUBB fuel, generation-asset, grid/equipment, and interconnection economics.

  • BE/PSIX/GNRC/CAT/FLNC/BLDP/PLUG bridge/resilience economics belong to Onsite Bridge Power, Storage, and Backup. STEM is retired and owns no current route.
  • ETN/POWL/HPS.A, NVTS/VICR/AEIS/BELFB, VRT/JCI/NVT, and PWR/EME site-entry-to-rack economics belong to Facility Electrical, Rack Power, Cooling, and Delivery.

docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 CEST Status: canonical spine for compute platforms and custom silicon. Primary ownership ends at architecture/platform/IP; it does not own foundry/package realization, physical memory/storage, networking/optical, or systems manufacturing.

docs.title: What this spine answers
docs.text: This page explains which compute architecture executes the workload: accelerators/GPUs, custom ASICs/XPUs, CPU/host compute, architecture/IP/EDA, system architecture, and edge/physical AI. Demand budget comes from Cloud and Compute Demand; the physical layer that feeds data to compute comes from Memory, Storage, and In-System Data Movement; chip manufacturing and packaging come from Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials.

docs.title: Six subnodes
docs.text: Node Value capture Current local anchors Key disconfirmation GPU / accelerator platform silicon + software + system/network attach NVDA, AMD, CBRS weak utilization/unit economics, platform substitution, supply ahead of demand Custom ASIC / XPU workload-specific performance/watt and design/service content AVGO, MRVL customer concentration, project cadence, merchant-platform catch-up CPU / host compute feeds/controls accelerators and general-purpose agent workloads AMD, INTC host share/ASP fails to grow with AI workload Architecture / IP / EDA design standards, IP royalty, ecosystem control ARM; EDA routes through current-live/query pages insourcing or failure of royalty/content growth System architecture scale-up/scale-out topology and rack-level design choices GPU/ASIC/CPU anchors; manufacturing belongs to spine 6 architecture proof does not become volume system demand Edge / physical AI endpoint/robotics/automotive inference optionality QCOM, TXN context datacenter narrative diverges from segment dollars

docs.title: Systems, Racks, and Complex Manufacturing
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 CEST Status: canonical spine 6. It primary-owns server/rack architecture, system integration, EMS/NPI, and complex network/optical manufacturing economics.

docs.title: What this spine answers
docs.text:
Qualified semiconductor packages, memory, networking/optical components, and power/cooling interfaces are not yet deployable AI capacity. This page asks who designs, procures, integrates, tests, and delivers them as servers, racks, network appliances, or complex optical/network systems—and how that delivery appears in revenue, margin, working capital, customer concentration, and service attach.

Its economics differ from spine 5. Spine 5 tracks wafer/package yield and test content; this page tracks program/NPI ramp, material availability, factory utilization, inventory/receivables, mix, customer bargaining power, and delivery margin.

docs.title: Four subnodes
docs.text: Node Problem solved Primary anchors Key disconfirmation Server / rack architecture and integration combines compute, memory, network, power/cooling, software, and support into sellable systems DELL AI backlog/revenue fails to become margin, cash conversion, or service attach; PC/legacy mix masks economics Design / HPS / system manufacturing hyperscaler/custom-platform design, switch/storage/system assembly, and engineering CLS HPS growth is not durable, customer concentration rises, or capex/working capital consumes returns EMS / NPI / rack-scale complex build PCB/backplane/cable/test, new-product introduction, rack-scale assembly, and supply-chain orchestration SANM named program/volume remains open or generic EMS mix caps margin Optical / network complex manufacturing process control, yield, test, and volume delivery for complex modules/systems FN datacom mix/customer concentration, pricing, capacity utilization, or execution reverses

docs.title: Delivery map
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C["Compute package"]
    M["Memory / storage"]
    N["Network / optical components"]
    P["Power / cooling interfaces"]
    D["Design + NPI + supply chain"]
    A["Assembly + test + yield"]
    R["Deployable server / rack / network system"]
    F["Revenue + margin + working capital + cash"]

    C --> D
    M --> D
    N --> D
    P --> D
    D --> A --> R --> F

Upstream components may improve together, but a delay in NPI, materials, test, rack integration, or the site interface can still defer system revenue and cash conversion.

docs.title: Evidence ladder
docs.text:
• Proven: issuer disclosure gives AI/cloud/HPS/datacom program revenue/backlog, a named design/customer/partner, production shipment, margin, or cash/working-capital evidence.
  • Issuer claim: guidance/outlook, capability, pipeline, TAM, future factory/capacity, or future launch.
  • Reasonable inference: higher rack complexity raises integration, test, supply-chain orchestration, and service attach; program-level economics still need proof.
  • Not proven: every EMS is an AI beneficiary; component demand automatically becomes system margin; a named ecosystem equals a volume purchase; backlog equals FCF.

docs.title: Primary ownership and outbound routing
docs.text:
• This page primary-owns DELL/CLS/SANM/FN system and complex-manufacturing economics. Networking, compute, packaging, and facility pages may secondary-link them but must not duplicate the primary parent.
  • Wafer/foundry/package/bonding/inspection/probe/test/KGD/substrate/materials belong to Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials.
  • Fabric/interconnect semis/optical engines/DCI product ownership belongs to AI Interconnect, Optical Networking, and DCI. FN/SANM appear there only as demand-side links.
  • Site-entry electrical, rack/board power, cooling, controls, and EPC/MEP belong to Facility Electrical, Rack Power, Cooling, and Delivery. This page owns only the system-side interface and delivery.

docs.title: AAOI — Applied Optoelectronics
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 Industry page: AI Interconnect, Optical Networking, and DCI Action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: AAOI's core business is manufacturing data-center optical transceivers and vertically integrated optical components. It sells high-speed optical connectivity, not switching systems or full network stacks.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text:
• Its primary role is a hyperscale data-center optical transceiver / module supplier.
  • Its AI relevance comes mainly from 800G and 1.6T optical-module shipments and capacity ramps.
  • The company sells modules and components, not network-system ownership.
  • Current proof is concentrated in a small number of hyperscale customer programs, so concentration sits inside the role boundary.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: AI-network upgrades first show up as 800G and 1.6T module orders, volume shipments, and capacity ramps, then flow into AAOI revenue. That bridge has appeared, but customer diversification and profit quality are not yet proven at the same level.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Q1 2026 revenue was USD 151.1M, and the company disclosed the first volume shipment of 800G products to a large hyperscale customer.
  • At the end of Q1 2026, 800G transceiver monthly capacity was nearly 100,000 units.
  • The company disclosed that top ten customers represented 98% of Q1 revenue, and that accounts receivable included USD 222.7M due from Digicomm International Inc.
  • The Amazon-linked customer warrant covers up to 7,945,399 shares, combining customer validation with potential dilution.
  • The 2026-04-02 release disclosed a new USD 71M 800G transceiver order, bringing orders from the same major hyperscale customer to USD 124M since mid-March; the company also disclosed shipping the first 10,000 800G units to another hyperscale customer.
  • The 2026-06-17 release disclosed the first volume order for 1.6T data-center transceivers from a long-term major hyperscale customer.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Q2 FY2026 outlook was revenue of USD 180M-198M and non-GAAP gross margin of 29%-30%.
  • Management said growth should increase further in Q3 as additional capacity comes online.
  • The company said combined 800G / 1.6T monthly capacity could exceed 500,000 units by the end of 2026 and that it expects to soon have the largest related capacity in the U.S.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• AAOI has moved from former-half-hidden into Market-found because issuer-primary evidence has progressed from order language to volume shipment and revenue bridge.
  • It still is not a clean core compounder because customer concentration, dilution structure, and profit repair are not yet fully settled.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The page does not prove that AAOI has established durable multi-customer hyperscale share.
  • The page does not prove that the 800G / 1.6T ramp has turned into stable GAAP profitability.
  • The page also does not cleanly separate AI-related revenue from broader data-center optical revenue.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If 800G / 1.6T orders stop converting into shipments, revenue, or capacity utilization, the page's AI-to-revenue logic should be downgraded.
  • If customer concentration and potential dilution keep rising while profit quality fails to improve, AAOI's durable role should not be upgraded.
  • If the expansion story remains only issuer claim without broader customer follow-through, this page should stay cautious.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: active / Market-found; modifier: former-half-hidden. It is now a market-found optical-module name, but it still needs to be read through concentration risk and in-progress profit validation.

docs.text: Last updated: 2026-04-16 02:45 CEST Industry page: Platform Technology, Internet, and Distribution Classification: direct

docs.title: Theme position
docs.text: Device entry, operating system, services ecosystem, and on-device AI.

docs.title: Why it belongs in this theme
docs.text: Apple’s moat is not single hardware, but the platform capability built from device base, distribution rights, paid services, and a developer ecosystem.

docs.title: My currently more credible bullish case
docs.text: The installed base continues to hit record highs, and Services keep producing high-quality cash flow. If Apple Intelligence keeps meaningfully improving upgrade reasons and ecosystem stickiness, platform value stays strong.

docs.title: My current top risks
docs.text: Growth is still sensitive to iPhone cycles; if AI experience is not clearly superior, the market will re-rate it back toward a mature hardware company. Regulatory pressure on App Store remains a constant.

docs.title: One-line view
docs.text: In this Platform setup, the hardware entry remains strong and Services plus private AI improve stickiness, but growth remains constrained by refresh cadence.

docs.title: ADTN — ADTRAN Holdings
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 Industry page: AI Interconnect, Optical Networking, and DCI Action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: ADTRAN is a broadband / access equipment company that also owns optical-networking and DCI assets. It is not a pure AI-optics company and not a pure hyperscaler-module vendor.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text:
• Its primary role is an optical transport / DCI platform inside a broader broadband / access company.
  • Its secondary role is intra-data-center AI adjacency through LiteWave800 and related 800G products.
  • The company is not a pure AI-optics pure play and not a clean hyperscaler optical winner.
  • The main boundary today is that product language exists, but AI revenue / customer proof is still not closed.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: If ADTN eventually turns AI into revenue, the path would run through optical networking, coherent / DCI, and intra-data-center connectivity products. The current sources do not disclose a named AI customer, a design win, a volume shipment, or an AI-revenue breakout.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Issuer-primary materials continue to describe the business across metro optical transport, data center interconnect, and broadband access.
  • The 2026-07-07 source refresh still references hyper-scalers, neocloud, content providers, and data-center companies, showing that the company explicitly covers that customer context in product positioning.
  • Customer / ecosystem materials show real optical / DCI deployment and interoperability references, including Openreach, Titan 800G, and OIF ZR / ZR+ materials.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• The Q1 exhibit describes LiteWave800 as the first product purpose-built for intra-data-center AI infrastructure at 800G.
  • Product and source-refresh materials place the company in a dynamic AI network cloud / DCI context.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• ADTN can still remain in the optical / DCI adjacency layer because the product and ecosystem evidence show that this is not an empty story.
  • It can only remain active / Needs-source for now. The proof-first modifier has to stay because there is still a visible gap between product language and disclosed revenue.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The page does not have named AI-customer, design-win, or volume-shipment evidence showing that LiteWave800 or related FSP / DCI products have reached AI-data-center volume.
  • The page does not have an issuer-primary AI / DCI revenue breakout.
  • The page also does not prove that optical / DCI relevance is strong enough to overpower the broader broadband / access story.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If later issuer-primary material still contains only product positioning and no additional customer or revenue proof, ADTN's AI-adjacency role should keep losing weight.
  • If the optical / DCI story stays only roadmap or positioning language, this page should not be upgraded into a stronger Market-found role.
  • If the company still has to be understood mainly as a broadband / access recovery with no cleaner optical proof, the page should remain proof-first or leave the main tracking layer.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: active / Needs-source; modifier: proof-first. It is an optical / DCI adjacency name, not a proven AI-optical revenue owner.

docs.title: AEIS — Advanced Energy Industries
docs.text:
Updated: 2026-07-13

Industry page: AI Interconnect, Optical Networking, and DCI

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: AEIS is an Active / Market-found precision / high-density power conversion company with the body-only modifier former-half-hidden. It sits between the site electrical boundary and the energized rack, converting incoming power into rack-usable power, but it does not own E7 generation, E2 compute silicon, or E6 full systems.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text:
AEIS sits after the site electrical boundary and before the energized rack. Its core exposure is power shelves, front-end AC-DC conversion, and power management for higher-density racks.

Its boundary needs to stay explicit: - It does not own E7 generation / grid / time-to-power assets and should not be written up as a generation or utility-power owner. - It does not own E2 compute silicon, so GPU or ASIC demand cannot be treated as AEIS revenue by default. - It does not own E6 systems integration, so full rack, server, or site delivery should not be attributed to AEIS.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text:
As AI servers and liquid-cooled high-density racks push cabinet power higher, OEM, ODM, and hyperscale platforms need denser rack-entry power and higher-performance conversion. AEIS monetizes that through data-center power products rather than through broad "AI exposure" language.

That mechanism still has to stay under issuer-claim discipline: the company has proven product and revenue exposure in the data-center power-conversion layer, but it has not fully closed the loop on named AI customers, exact rack platforms, or attributable revenue by program.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• AEIS identifies data center computing as an important end market in its 10-K and results materials, and that business already contributes visible revenue.
  • Public company materials and OCP / ORv3 product evidence show AEIS providing rack-entry power shelf, front-end conversion, and high-density power-management capability.
  • The company has already disclosed Data Center Computing as one of the faster-growing revenue lines, so the exposure is not just conceptual mapping.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Management framing supports the idea that AI infrastructure power upgrades can expand AEIS's data-center power business.
  • Management framing also supports product fit for higher power density, liquid cooling, and next-generation rack power architectures.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• If hyperscalers and OEMs keep moving to higher-power rack architectures, AEIS can continue to benefit at the rack-entry conversion layer.
  • The revenue elasticity is more likely to come from power shelves, front-end conversion, and adjacent power-management penetration than from any single chip cycle.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• It is not yet proven that AEIS has attributable revenue from a named hyperscaler or server platform inside a major AI cluster.
  • It is not yet proven how much of the incremental data-center revenue is specifically AI rather than broader cloud or enterprise power refresh.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If later issuer-primary or SEC documents weaken the importance of Data Center Computing to growth, this page should be downgraded.
  • If the product position turns out to be mostly generic industrial power rather than high-density rack-entry power, the core framing should be rewritten.
  • If new evidence shows AI capex moving toward electrical architectures where AEIS has little exposure, the role strength needs to be reassessed.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text:
Active / Market-found; modifier: former-half-hidden. The E8 role is precision / high-density power conversion from the site electrical boundary to the energized rack, with a hard boundary at not owning E7 generation, E2 compute silicon, or E6 systems.

docs.title: AFRM — Affirm Holdings
docs.text: Role: E10 cross-theme BNPL merchant-network and consumer-credit owner Structural status: active Formal discovery state: Market-found Updated: 2026-07-13; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Affirm places merchant distribution, consumer installments, and pay-over-time products inside one payment-network framework. Core revenue comes from merchant, transaction/network, and consumer-credit economics rather than a standalone AI revenue line.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: AFRM belongs to the E10 cross-theme fintech portfolio, not an AI or data-center supply spine. It owns the BNPL merchant-network and consumer-credit role. It does not absorb SOFI's digital-bank and lending platform, HOOD's retail-brokerage and crypto entry point, or a generic application or infrastructure-owner role.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: The current local issuer packet provides no standalone AI/ML monetization proof. If AI/ML supports underwriting, fraud, servicing, or productivity, value still has to appear in approval quality, loss performance, merchant conversion, cost, or network economics. This page does not place it in the realized revenue bridge before direct evidence exists.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Official IR materials and the FY2026 Q2 results define Affirm as a payment network connecting consumers and merchants.
  • The local packet treats Active Consumers and GMV as operating metrics and places merchant-growth tools and pay-over-time products in one framework. Those are network and credit anchors, not AI revenue.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Company framing emphasizes the payment network and pay-over-time products that help consumers and merchants grow.
  • The local packet contains no management metric that can be promoted into standalone AI monetization.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• Better risk decisioning, fraud control, or servicing could improve approvals, losses, and merchant economics.
  • That inference can be upgraded only when direct issuer evidence ties model capability to verifiable operating results.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• AI/ML has created separately trackable revenue, profit, or paid attach.
  • Broad GMV, Active Consumer, or merchant growth is directly attributable to AI.
  • AFRM should absorb SOFI, HOOD, or a wider application or infrastructure role.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• Deteriorating credit losses, funding costs, or capital-market availability would weaken network economics.
  • If merchant and consumer growth does not become healthy take rate and credit performance, scale alone is not enough.
  • If direct model-to-outcome evidence remains absent, AI/ML stays an unproven support mechanism.
