docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Datadog makes money from observability, security, logs, APM, cloud monitoring, and developer-tooling subscriptions and usage. Its core spine-9 role is providing a billable observation and control layer for runtime, telemetry, debugging, and security response once AI and cloud workloads move into production, not owning the application, data, or infrastructure itself.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: DDOG primary-owns the observability / security runtime layer in AI Application Production and Data Lifecycle, while remaining adjacent to developer-tooling distribution in Platform Technology, Internet, and Distribution. It is not an application owner, data/context owner, E2 silicon owner, E6 systems owner, or E7/E8 physical-infrastructure owner. It controls the failure point of continuous observation, debugging, and protection after a workload is deployed.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: As AI and cloud workloads expand, customers generate more telemetry, logs, traces, GPU monitoring, security analysis, and adjacent product attach. Datadog gets paid through monitored objects, data ingestion, product expansion, and platform adoption. Broad cloud spend, broad revenue, or customer count do not automatically equal AI revenue.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Q1 2026 revenue was USD 1.006B, up 32% year over year.
  • USD 100K+ ARR customers were about 4,550, versus about 3,770 a year earlier, up 21%.
  • Operating cash flow was USD 335M; free cash flow was USD 289M.
  • The local 2026-06-28 SEC latest-route packet shows that subsequent locally visible filings were mainly Form 4 / 144 routes, with no newer operating print added to this page's source set.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• FY2026 revenue guidance is about USD 4.30B-4.32B.
  • The local raw packet records MCP Server, Bits AI Security Agent, GPU Monitoring, Experiments, and broader AI observability / security positioning.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text: If AI and cloud workloads keep increasing telemetry density, incident complexity, and debugging demand, Datadog can expand monetization through more product attach and higher usage.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The company does not separately disclose AI revenue. Broad revenue, ARR customer tiers, or total observability spend are not automatically AI monetization.
  • Product launches and positioning still need finer attach-rate, retention, and workload-mix proof before AI observability can be treated as a separate budget line.

docs.title: Value capture and misread boundary
docs.text: DDOG captures value through cross-cloud telemetry, AI workload observability, and security attach, not by owning application logic, enterprise data context, or physical compute. The easiest misread is to treat any GPU/LLM deployment as Datadog revenue, or to blur observability into workflow/control-plane ownership.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• Cloud optimization or workload efficiency compresses telemetry growth and product expansion.
  • Platform bundling, open-source/self-hosted tooling, or hyperscaler-native monitoring weakens attach rates.
  • AI workload monitoring remains feature adoption rather than a durable budget line.
  • Security and observability cross-sell stops reinforcing itself, so product count and cash conversion stop improving together.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: DDOG is a Core / Market-found spine-9 observability / security owner.

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Dell designs, develops, manufactures, markets, sells, and supports infrastructure and client products. It reports through two segments: Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) and Client Solutions Group (CSG). The relevant piece here is ISG: AI-optimized servers, traditional servers and networking, storage, software, and deployment/support services.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: In spine 6, DELL is a branded systems and infrastructure delivery company. It is not a generic ODM/EMS, and it is not a single-component bottleneck owner. Its boundary is the packaged delivery of servers, networking, storage, and related services; upstream chip, optics, or component economics should not be assigned to DELL by default.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text:
• Q4 FY2026 disclosed more than USD 64B of full-year AI-optimized server orders, more than USD 25B of full-year shipments, and USD 43B of opening FY2027 backlog.
  • Q1 FY2027 disclosed USD 24.4B of AI orders booked and USD 16.1B of AI server revenue recognized; within that, AI-optimized servers revenue was USD 16.132B, up 757% year over year.
  • In the same quarter, ISG revenue was USD 29.009B, including USD 8.543B of traditional servers and networking revenue, up 92% year over year. That shows AI revenue is already recognized at the server layer while broader infrastructure content is also growing.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• The 10-K states that DELL is organized around ISG and CSG; ISG addresses AI, machine learning, data analytics, and multicloud with integrated infrastructure solutions.
  • Q4 FY2026 disclosed >USD 64B of AI server orders, >USD 25B of AI server shipments for the year, and USD 43B of opening FY2027 backlog.
  • Q1 FY2027 disclosed USD 16.132B of AI-optimized server revenue, USD 29.009B of ISG revenue, USD 8.543B of traditional servers and networking revenue, and 10.5% ISG operating margin.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• In management commentary, Dell says enterprise and sovereign customers are increasing AI spending and that Dell AI Factories include networking, storage, and professional services.
  • The FY2027 AI-optimized server revenue target of roughly USD 60B is guidance, not a proven outcome.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• DELL monetizes AI through branded server and infrastructure system delivery and should no longer be framed only as a legacy PC company.
  • Traditional servers and networking also grew strongly in the same quarter as AI server scale-up, which likely means AI demand is pulling through broader system content. The exact attach mix is still not broken out.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The revenue split for AI-driven storage, networking, and services.
  • Quarter-by-quarter stability of backlog conversion into revenue.
  • The sustainable margin profile of the AI systems business across changing customer and component mixes.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• AI orders and backlog stop converting into recognized revenue for multiple quarters.
  • ISG margins deteriorate materially while AI mix rises, implying DELL is mainly a low-value pass-through.
  • Large customers shift AI-factory-level system integration to other system vendors or in-house designs, weakening DELL's delivery role.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: Core / Market-found branded systems/infrastructure anchor in spine 6. The point of watching DELL is to verify that AI server and full-system infrastructure revenue is truly landing at the systems layer, not to rewrite it as a generic ODM.

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: DigitalOcean sells compute, storage, managed cloud, and AI infrastructure to developers, SMBs, and digital-native customers through subscriptions and usage. In spine 9, it is better treated as an alternative cloud-compute benchmark for smaller-scale AI app runtime, not as a hyperscaler, application/data owner, or physical-infrastructure owner.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: DOCN primary-owns the developer / inference runtime benchmark inside AI Application Production and Data Lifecycle, while remaining adjacent to smaller-scale cloud capacity in Cloud and Compute Demand. It is not a hyperscale demand anchor, does not primary-own the application/data layer, does not primary-own E2 silicon or E6 systems, and does not own E7/E8 physical infrastructure. This page keeps only the alternative-runtime mechanism and unit-economics boundary.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: Paperspace, GPU/AI compute, storage, and managed-service usage become recurring ARR and consumption revenue only when customers actually use that runtime. AI turns into revenue through inference/runtime usage, customer attach, and capacity utilization. Broad ARR, broad cloud revenue, or committed capacity are not automatically AI revenue.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Q1 2026 revenue was USD 258M, up 22%; ARR was USD 1.032B, up 22%.
  • AI Customer ARR was USD 170M, up 221%; Million+ Dollar Customer ARR was USD 183M, up 179%.
  • RPO was USD 243M, versus USD 14M a year earlier.
  • Adjusted EBITDA was USD 105M / 41%.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• The 2026-07-07 preliminary update expected Q2 revenue growth of about 29%, RPO above USD 800M/more than 10x YoY, weighted contract duration above three years, and multiple nine-figure annual commitments. These are issuer preliminary claims, not a full Q2 filing.
  • Total committed capacity is about 155MW; a new 20MW is expected in late 2027/early 2028.
  • The issuer says 81% of Q1 AI Customer ARR came from inference services and core cloud rather than bare-metal GPU rental. The definition still includes the customer's broader cloud revenue and is not pure AI-product ARR.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text: Developer-first distribution and an integrated AI-native stack may win inference/agent workloads that do not require full hyperscaler complexity.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text: USD 800M+ RPO is not automatically incremental revenue or take-or-pay. Top-customer concentration, cancellation rights, the next-12-month portion and capacity-level margin remain undisclosed. 155MW is not full utilization or realized cash economics.

docs.title: Value capture and misread boundary
docs.text: DOCN captures value through developer-first runtime, price/performance, and a simpler AI app deployment surface, not through hyperscaler-scale demand ownership, application/data ownership, or physical buildout ownership. The easiest misread is to label all developer-cloud growth as AI runtime revenue, or to treat committed capacity as already realized cash economics.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• AI ARR, large-customer ARR, or RPO conversion decelerates repeatedly.
  • The 155MW capacity is delayed, underutilized, or requires excess financing; disclosed and post-quarter facility obligations total roughly USD 1.94B while Q1 adjusted FCF margin was only 1%.
  • Hyperscalers, neo-clouds, or inference platforms create price/performance pressure.
  • The final share count, price, note repurchase and hedge/capped-call treatment in the 2026-07-15 transaction weaken per-share claims; do not call it dilution-free deleveraging before final terms.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: DOCN is a Context / Market-found spine-9 alternative cloud-compute benchmark.

docs.title: EME — EMCOR Group
docs.text: Role: Phase 5 E8 spine 8 site electrical boundary to energized rack; EME is the MEP / EPC installation benchmark Structural status: context Formal discovery state: Market-found Evidence through: 2026-04-19; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: EMCOR is not a platform selling electrical gear or cooling hardware. It is the construction and services organization that actually delivers the room's electrical, mechanical, fire, low-voltage, and operations stack. In E8 it benchmarks mission-critical MEP / EPC delivery capability rather than equipment ownership.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: EME covers the mission-critical installation and delivery layer after the site electrical boundary: electrical construction, mechanical construction, HVAC, plumbing, fire protection, low voltage, commissioning, facilities support, and operational readiness. It does not own upstream generation / fuel, and it does not own E6 servers / network systems. It sells build / install / maintain work, not generation assets, servers, or network equipment themselves.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: AI campus expansion eventually becomes real project execution. EME monetizes that through data-center design, core and shell work, prefabrication, electrical / mechanical installation, backup power, advanced cooling, commissioning, and Day 2 operations support. AI matters here because it raises mission-critical construction and services demand, not because EMCOR gets a hardware ASP.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• EMCOR's mission-critical page explicitly says it delivers end-to-end data-center solutions including infrastructure design and build, low-voltage installation, fire protection, and ongoing operations and maintenance.
  • The same page defines the full-lifecycle scope as initial design, core and shell construction, prefabrication, hardware installation, and ongoing maintenance and monitoring.
  • The electrical-construction section explicitly includes redundant back-up power systems, electrical distribution, and switchyards and switchgears.
  • The mechanical-construction section explicitly includes advanced cooling systems, HVAC, plumbing, fabrication, equipment installation, monitoring, and maintenance.
  • EMCOR also states it can provide 24/7/365 on-site mechanical and electrical systems support plus operational readiness and server / switchgear / router installation.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• EMCOR positions itself as a nationwide organization able to build, power, service, and protect data centers in highly regulated mission-critical environments.
  • Management language emphasizes full-lifecycle delivery and hyperscale mobilization capability, but the current raw packet does not directly attribute guidance or RPO to data centers as a standalone end market.
  • FY2025 Q4 results disclosed company-wide Remaining Performance Obligations of USD 13.25B, up 31.2% year over year, and 2026 revenue guidance of USD 17.75B–18.50B; those company-wide figures are not proof of AI or data-center revenue.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• If the AI buildout bottleneck is simply getting campuses built and kept operational, EMCOR-type MEP / EPC installers and service organizations are real beneficiaries.
  • Its economics are still construction-and-services economics, not the equipment-owner economics of cooling hardware, electrical gear, or server systems.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The current raw packet does not provide data-center revenue share, mission-critical backlog / RPO split, or AI-project margin uplift.
  • There is also no evidence yet that EMCOR captures materially above-normal profit structure from AI data-center delivery versus ordinary large-project contracting.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• The mission-critical data-center capability is real, but if later filings still do not break out revenue / backlog / margin contribution, EMCOR should remain only a benchmark rather than move into higher-conviction status.
  • If hyperscale buildout slows or price competition compresses construction margins, EMCOR's AI read-through is more fragile than that of equipment platforms.
  • If critical scope shifts toward more vertical cooling, electrical, or modular specialists, EMCOR's bridge role in delivery weakens.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: EME is the Context / Market-found MEP / EPC installation benchmark inside E8. It represents mission-critical build / install / maintain capability; it does not own E7 generation / fuel or E6 servers / network systems.

docs.title: ENTG — Entegris
docs.text: Role: spine 5 manufacturing / packaging / test / materials active; materials / purity / contamination-control support layer Structural status: active Formal discovery state: Needs-source Evidence through: 2026-04-30; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Entegris mainly sells semiconductor materials plus filtration, purity, and contamination-control solutions. Its AI relevance comes from more complex advanced manufacturing and advanced packaging raising the need for purity, substrate integrity, and yield support, but it is not a direct packaging-equipment owner and the monetization bridge is still incomplete.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: ENTG primary-owns the materials / purity / contamination-control support layer inside Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials. It is not an OSAT, not an inspection / metrology tool, and not a direct compute platform; this page can only write it as a support layer for advanced manufacturing and advanced packaging.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: As device architectures, heterogeneous integration, and advanced packaging become more complex, customers need more purity, materials performance, substrate management, and yield support. ENTG's revenue bridge is currently proven only to the level of advanced manufacturing processes plus AI-related demand improving order patterns; it is not yet proven to a separate advanced-packaging / AI revenue split.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Q1 2026 net sales were $811.9M, up 5% YoY; non-GAAP diluted EPS was $0.86.
  • The same Q1 raw said revenue growth was primarily driven by unit-driven volumes related to the industry's most advanced manufacturing processes.
  • The Q4 2025 raw said 2025 unit-driven growth came from ongoing strength in liquid filtration, selective etch, and CMP consumables in the most advanced technologies.
  • Materials Solutions provides deposition materials, CMP slurries and pads, specialty gases, and etch / clean materials; Advanced Purity Solutions provides filtration, purification, and contamination control.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Q1 2026 management said semiconductor demand continues to improve, AI-related demand is accelerating, and order patterns are strengthening; these are management attribution and trend claims.
  • Q4 2025 management said complex device architectures support AI growth and create higher content-per-wafer, purity, and yield-support opportunities; this remains forward opportunity framing.
  • The company positions its materials, filtration, and purification products as improving yield, device reliability, and purity, and says heterogeneous integration needs advanced materials, delivery, ESD, and substrate-management solutions.
  • Q2 2026 guidance was sales of $815M-$845M and non-GAAP EPS of $0.76-$0.84; that remains forward-looking guidance.
  • Q4 2025 commentary about growth acceleration, higher content per wafer, and sustained market outperformance also remains issuer forward framing.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text: ENTG is a real materials and yield-support layer for more complex AI-era manufacturing / advanced packaging, but its exposure is still indirect. The cleanest current write-up is “the support layer is real,” not “this is already a high-purity advanced-packaging monetization name.”

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• Advanced-packaging revenue, AI revenue, and HBM-related mix are not separately disclosed.
  • Named-customer or program-level advanced-packaging monetization proof is not disclosed.
  • It is not proven which exact product lines are driving the AI-related demand improvement.
  • It is not proven that ENTG deserves higher conviction than purer equipment, test, or inspection names.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• The AI-related-demand and order-pattern-improvement language disappears without better segment evidence replacing it.
  • Advanced-packaging product positioning stays at the capability-showcase level instead of converting into verifiable content / yield economics.
  • Unit-driven growth at advanced nodes and high-complexity manufacturing stalls.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: ENTG is an Active / Needs-source materials / purity support name. Keeping it in the wiki is reasonable, but any upgrade in conviction requires company-level advanced-packaging / AI monetization proof rather than an automatic extrapolation from broad materials importance.

docs.title: ETN — Eaton
docs.text: Role: Phase 5 E8 spine 8 site electrical boundary to energized rack; ETN is the broad electrical / UPS / switchgear benchmark Structural status: context Formal discovery state: Market-found Evidence through: 2026-05-05; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Eaton is a large electrical platform spanning site-entry electrical, internal power distribution, power quality, modular power enclosures, and thermal adjacencies. It is not a single-theme data-center pure play. In E8 it is the benchmark used to calibrate broad electrical / UPS / switchgear exposure.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: ETN sits after the site electrical boundary and before the energized rack: power distribution, power quality, circuit protection, utility power distribution, services, cooling products, structural support systems, plus Fibrebond modular power enclosures. It does not own upstream generation / fuel, and it does not own E6 servers / network systems.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: When hyperscalers or colos expand capacity, AI-related spend first lands in site-entry electrical, distribution, power quality, and modular power enclosures. ETN's current monetization comes from selling its existing electrical platform and Fibrebond modular-power capability into data-center, utility, and industrial end markets.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• The FY2025 annual report and Q1 2026 10-Q define Eaton as an intelligent power management company serving data center, utility, industrial, commercial, and other end markets.
  • Management says Eaton is deepening participation across the electrical power value chain and benefiting from momentum in data-center and utility end markets.
  • Electrical Americas / Electrical Global products explicitly include power distribution and assemblies, power quality, circuit protection, utility power distribution, services, cooling products, and structural support systems.
  • Fibrebond is described as designing and building pre-integrated modular power enclosures for data-center and other customers.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Eaton presents itself as a broad electrical platform serving multiple end markets rather than a narrow data-center subcategory.
  • The Boyd transaction language describes the target as a thermal-components and systems leader and says that, if completed, the deal would help serve hyperscale / colocation customers from chip to grid. That shows management wants critical liquid cooling inside the same electrical-platform story, but it is not proof of a completed portfolio expansion.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• Within E8, ETN is more useful as a benchmark than as a sharp mispricing call because it spans site power distribution, power quality, and modular power enclosures across the site-entry electrical bucket.
  • Its revenue base remains broad industrial and electrical exposure, so ETN should not be framed as a pure-play AI data-center winner.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The current raw packet does not break out ETN's data-center revenue, UPS mix, or the standalone profit contribution of switchgear / cooling.
  • It is not yet proven that Fibrebond synergies or data-center exposure will durably change Eaton's growth profile across more reporting periods.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• Data-center and utility end-market momentum weakens enough to cool the AI read-through for the broad electrical platform.
  • Fibrebond modular power fails to show up in clearer order, revenue, or profit structure.
  • If ETN's data-center exposure remains only a broad-platform narrative without better attach-rate / mix evidence, the benchmark role should not be mistaken for a higher-conviction hidden thesis.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: ETN is the Context / Market-found broad electrical / UPS / switchgear benchmark inside E8. It calibrates inside-the-fence electrical-platform exposure; it does not own E7 generation / fuel or E6 servers / network systems.

docs.title: FLNC — Fluence Energy
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 Industry page: Onsite Bridge Power, Storage, and Backup Action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Fluence Energy's core business is battery energy storage systems, control software, and related services. It sells bridge storage, backup, and power-quality tools, not utility-generation asset ownership.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text:
• It belongs to the Phase 5 E7 onsite / bridge storage segment inside the generation / grid / time-to-power causal lane.
  • The role boundary stops at storage, controls, and faster energization. It does not extend into site electrical distribution, rack power, cooling, or EPC spine 8.
  • Fluence's storage systems are not a utility-generation owner and are not a long-duration baseload owner.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: If AI data centers need faster interconnection, phased energization, backup, or power-quality support, Fluence can turn those needs into revenue through storage systems, control software, and project services. That path is a bridge / backup mechanism, not long-term generation ownership.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• The local product capture directly places Fluence storage solutions in the data-center use case.
  • The local issuer-primary case capture includes a Fluence / Centrica / Google Belgium backup-related example.
  • The local 10-Q and results captures are sufficient to establish that the company sells storage systems and software, not a generic theme proxy.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• The company presents storage for data-center use cases as faster deployment, interconnection support, backup, and power quality.
  • Company materials place storage in a bridge role for data-center power rather than in a primary baseload role.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• FLNC is best treated as Phase 5 E7 context because it helps define the boundary between storage exposure and onsite generation exposure.
  • It has a real lane use case, but it is closer to bridge storage than to onsite generation ownership.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The page does not isolate AI-only revenue, AI-only backlog, or data-center-only storage revenue.
  • The page does not prove that data-center storage has become broad and repeatable enough to upgrade FLNC into a mainline core name.
  • The page also does not prove that storage here is the long-duration baseload role rather than the bridge / backup role.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If future issuer-primary or filing evidence stops connecting Fluence storage systems to data-center bridge, backup, or interconnection use cases, this page's role should be downgraded.
  • If the current examples remain showcase-only and fail to produce repeat booking, deployment, or revenue evidence, the AI-to-revenue logic should be rewritten.
  • If the data-center narrative effectively collapses back into generic grid storage rather than the onsite / time-to-power lane, this page should leave Phase 5 E7 mainline tracking.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: Context / Needs-source. Proof gates: 1. Issuer-primary or filing evidence for named data-center storage deployment or contract scope. 2. Repeatable data-center revenue, backlog, or booking evidence. 3. Clear proof that the role remains bridge / backup / interconnection rather than generic grid storage.

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Fabrinet provides advanced optical packaging and precision optical, electro-mechanical, and electronic manufacturing services for complex-product OEMs. It spans process design, engineering, supply chain, manufacturing, advanced packaging, integration, final assembly, and testing, with its core strength in high-complexity optical communications manufacturing.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: In spine 6, FN is a complex-optics manufacturing and interconnect exposure. It is not a branded systems vendor, and it is not a generic rack or full-system integrator. Its boundary is the manufacturing conversion of optical communication components, modules, and subsystems; it should not be collapsed into the same ODM label as the server/rack integration cases of CLS and SANM.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text:
• FY2025 total revenue was USD 3.419B, of which optical communications contributed USD 2.619B, or 76.6%; within that, datacom was USD 1.156B and telecom was USD 1.463B.
  • Q3 FY2026 revenue was USD 1.2143B, up 39.3% year over year.
  • In the Q3 FY2026 results, management said growth was supported by numerous ongoing and ramping programs and that new customer agreements, particularly in datacom, should strengthen growth into Q4 and beyond.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• The 10-K explicitly defines Fabrinet as an advanced optical packaging and precision opto-electronic manufacturing services provider for complex-product OEMs.
  • FY2025 disclosed that optical communications accounted for 76.6% of revenue, with separate revenue lines for datacom and telecom.
  • Q3 FY2026 disclosed USD 1.2143B of revenue, up 39.3% year over year, and explicitly mentioned new customer agreements in datacom.
  • Customer concentration is high in FY2025: NVIDIA represented about 27.6% of revenue and Cisco about 18.2%.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• The statement that new datacom customer agreements should strengthen growth into Q4 and beyond is forward-looking management language, not a proven outcome.
  • The Q2 FY2025 management commentary about datacenter interconnect demand and next-generation product ramps is also management guidance on demand cadence.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• FN's AI exposure comes mainly through datacom and optical manufacturing demand rather than through directly selling AI servers or owning the network-systems brand.
  • As AI expands from training clusters into broader scale-out and interconnect buildouts, a high-complexity optical manufacturer like FN is more likely to keep participating, but what it captures is manufacturing and yield value rather than full-system control.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• How much of datacom revenue can be strictly attributed to AI rather than broader optical communications demand.
  • Which specific customers or programs map to DCI versus other optical communications scenarios.
  • The duration of the current datacom ramp and the pace of diversification beyond a few large customers.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• Datacom ramps slow materially without replacement customer agreements.
  • Customer concentration worsens further and single-customer volatility starts to damage revenue quality.
  • Capacity expansion, yields, or delivery execution break down and weaken FN's credibility in high-complexity optical manufacturing.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: Active / Market-found complex optical manufacturing exposure in spine 6. It carries a former-half-hidden modifier, but that modifier belongs only in the body: the existence of revenue is no longer hidden; the remaining hidden piece is customer/program attribution and duration.

docs.title: FORM — FormFactor
docs.text: Role: spine 5 manufacturing / packaging / test / materials active; FORM owns the probe-card / wafer-probe / test-interface exposure Structural status: active Formal discovery state: Market-found Evidence through: 2026-05-14; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: FormFactor mainly makes money from probe cards, wafer probe, and related test interfaces. Its AI relevance is not packaging outsourcing; it is the way HBM and more complex advanced packages raise the value of precision probing, thermal handling, and known-good-die discipline.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: FORM primary-owns the probe-card / wafer-probe / test-interface node inside Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials. It is not an HBM memory maker, not an OSAT, and not a CoWoS owner; TER — Teradyne is the broader ATE benchmark instead.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: As HBM stacks, TSV, thermo-compression bonding, and larger AI packages increase test complexity, memory makers need higher-value probe cards and tighter KGD discipline. FORM's clearest revenue bridge currently sits inside the DRAM bucket, where the issuer directly tied growth to demand for HBM designs used in generative AI applications.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Q1 2026 revenue was USD 226.1M; Probe Cards revenue was USD 198.3M.
  • DRAM revenue was USD 82.93M, 36.7% of revenue, and up 69.7% YoY.
  • The issuer attributed DRAM growth primarily to increased demand for HBM designs used in generative AI applications, and the Q1 release also tied record DRAM revenue to HBM application demand.
  • The FY2025 10-K explicitly discussed DRAM including HBM and described packaging complexity tied to TSV and thermo-compression bonding.
  • The Q4 2024 release said FY2024 revenue growth was driven by HBM revenue growth and that HBM revenue increased fourfold versus the prior year.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text: • The current local raw packet does not provide a separate HBM revenue guide; any extension that HBM3E / HBM4 transitions will keep lifting FORM content should be treated as issuer framing until separately proven.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text: FORM remains one of the cleanest U.S.-listed HBM probe-card / KGD candidates because the issuer tied revenue growth directly to HBM / generative-AI design demand rather than to a generic semiconductor recovery. Versus a broad ATE platform, its test-interface exposure is purer.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• Absolute HBM revenue is not separately disclosed, and the DRAM bucket still includes non-HBM demand.
  • Customer concentration and HBM3E / HBM4 mix are not disclosed.
  • It is not proven that the Q1 growth rate can cleanly persist through memory capex, qualification cycles, and generation transitions.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• DRAM / HBM demand stops being cited directly as a growth driver.
  • Non-probe-card businesses dilute the AI / HBM economics again.
  • HBM generation transitions stop raising test value, or FORM loses critical share.
  • KGD / wafer-probe importance is reduced by customer insourcing, substitute flows, or a sharp cyclical reset.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: FORM is an Active / Market-found probe-card / test-interface name. It is an active owner inside spine 5 for HBM test complexity, but the thesis should stay anchored to test-interface economics rather than drifting into packaging outsourcing or broad ATE framing.

docs.title: GEV — GE Vernova
docs.text: Role: Phase 5 E7 spine 7 generation / grid / time-to-power; GEV owns the generation / grid equipment and service bridge Structural status: core Formal discovery state: Market-found Evidence through: 2026-04-22; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: GE Vernova is not a power seller or merchant generator owner. It is an industrial platform selling generation equipment, grid equipment, and long-term services. Its core revenue comes from Gas Power, Electrification, and related service contracts, while Wind remains a separate business and volatility source.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: Within Power Generation, Grid, and Fuel Supply, GEV primary-owns the generation / grid equipment and service bridge. It covers gas turbines, utility-side transformers, utility-side switchgear, AC substations, HVDC, and service contracts that help power projects reach the grid faster. Ownership stops at the site / utility handoff; inside-the-fence switchgear, rack power, cooling, EPC, and server / network layers do not belong here.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: As data-center demand tightens power availability, utilities, developers, and power customers order gas turbines, transformers, utility-side switchgear, substations, HVDC, and long-term services to compress time-to-power. GEV therefore monetizes AI through equipment and service orders plus backlog, not through electricity sales.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Official Q1 2026 materials disclosed USD 18.3B of orders, +71% organic growth, and USD 13.0B of sequential backlog growth.
  • Gas Power equipment backlog increased from 40 GW to 44 GW, while slot reservation agreements increased from 43 GW to 56 GW.
  • Electrification equipment backlog reached USD 38.6B, up 75% year over year; the company booked USD 2.4B of equipment orders to support data centers in the quarter, more than all of last year.
  • Management attributed Electrification growth to switchgear / transformers in Power Transmission and AC substation / HVDC solutions in Grid Systems Integration.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Management said demand is accelerating across both Power and Electrification and expects combined gas-turbine backlog plus slot reservations to reach at least 110 GW by year-end 2026.
  • The company describes the order momentum as coming from a diverse customer set, which implies data centers are a meaningful driver but not the only one.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• GEV is a bridge owner between generation buildout and grid connection, allowing it to capture early equipment and service spending when time-to-power becomes the bottleneck.
  • Revenue realization still depends on backlog conversion, delivery timing, and margin execution. Orders do not equal realized profit on day one.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• GEV's full Power / Electrification order book should not be treated as entirely AI-related, and current backlog should not be mechanically extrapolated into durable long-term margins.
  • The future share, delivery pace, and profit quality of data-center-related orders are not yet proven across a longer reporting history.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• Gas Power backlog / slot reservations materially stall, cancel, or stop converting into deliverable projects.
  • Data-center-related Electrification orders slow materially, or backlog-to-revenue / margin performance degrades persistently.
  • Utility-side power projects are materially delayed or scope shifts down into inside-the-fence system integration, weakening GEV's generation / grid bridge ownership.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: GEV is the Core / Market-found generation / grid equipment and service bridge on the generation spine. It is not the owner of electricity sales or inside-the-fence site power, cooling, or servers.

docs.title: GLW — Corning
docs.text: Role: spine 4 fiber / optical context; secondary exposure is materials-only context in spine 5 Structural status: context Formal discovery state: Needs-source Evidence through: 2026-07-02; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Corning earns from optical communications, specialty materials, display, and other diversified materials and connectivity businesses. Its AI relevance is real in fiber / cable / connectivity and plausibly real in advanced-packaging glass, but those economics are still buried inside large segments.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: GLW primary-owns the fiber / optical backbone exposure in AI Interconnect, Optical Networking, and DCI. It secondary-links to spine 5 materials context only through glass / specialty materials and owns none of that spine's manufacturing, packaging, or test nodes. It is also not an active-optics pure play.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: AI data centers need more fiber, cable, connectors, and data-center interconnect, so that demand should first land in Optical Communications. If customers adopt Corning’s ultra-flat / ultra-thin glass wafers and substrates for advanced semiconductor packaging, that optionality would sit inside Specialty Materials, but the product-level revenue bridge is still missing.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Corning’s 10-K explicitly says AI is driving strong demand for fiber and connectivity products inside and between data centers.
  • Optical Communications represented 38% of Corning’s 2025 total segment net sales.
  • Specialty Materials makes semiconductor optics including HPFS fused silica, ULE / EXTREME ULE, metrology instruments, custom optical assemblies, and ultra-flat, ultra-thin glass wafers and substrates for advanced semiconductor packaging; the segment represented 13% of 2025 total segment net sales.
  • NVIDIA and Corning announced a multiyear commercial and technology partnership focused on expanding U.S.-based advanced optical connectivity manufacturing.
  • Corning’s OFC 2026 materials introduced multicore fiber, micro cable, a 32-fiber MMC connector, and co-packaged optics systems positioned for AI network density, campus / long-distance interconnect, and larger AI networks.
  • Q1 2026 core sales grew 18% to USD 4.35B; Optical Communications sales grew 36%; the company attributed growth to demand for Gen AI products and new solar products.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Corning plans to increase U.S. optical connectivity manufacturing capacity 10x and U.S. fiber production capacity by >50%; that NVIDIA partnership buildout and Corning's OFC 2026 co-packaged-optics / new-connectivity launch set remain forward execution claims.
  • Corning describes itself as an end-to-end optical solutions platform from silicon to data center, but that is not a product-level revenue split.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text: Corning looks more like a lower-beta fiber / optical infrastructure beneficiary with secondary packaging-glass optionality than a high-purity active-optics or packaging-equipment name.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• NVIDIA partnership revenue contribution or customer concentration is not proven.
  • Advanced-packaging-glass revenue, customer list, utilization, or AI mix is not proven.
  • The share of Gen AI demand inside Optical Communications versus Specialty Materials is not proven.
  • It is not proven that GLW should primary-own the packaging lane.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• AI-driven Optical Communications demand normalizes without durable high-quality growth.
  • Capacity expansion and partnership activity fail to convert into profitable revenue.
  • Advanced-packaging glass stays optional rather than becoming a verifiable business.
  • Other large segments continue to swamp the optical / packaging signal.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: GLW is a Context / Needs-source fiber / optical backbone exposure name with secondary materials / packaging optionality. Current proof is enough to retain it, but not enough to write it as a higher-purity AI packaging or active-optics conclusion.

docs.title: GNRC — Generac
docs.text: Updated: 2026-07-13 Industry page: Onsite Bridge Power, Storage, and Backup Action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Generac's core business is backup generators, behind-the-meter energy systems, and control integration. It sells bridge / backup power equipment, not utility-generation asset ownership.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text:
• It belongs to the Phase 5 E7 backup and bridge-power-equipment segment inside the generation / grid / time-to-power causal lane.
  • The role boundary stops at gensets, storage integration, and controls. It does not extend into site electrical distribution, rack power, cooling, or EPC spine 8.
  • GNRC is a bridge / backup equipment mechanism, not a proven AI pure play and not a utility-generation owner.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: If hyperscale, colo, or campus customers need backup power, behind-the-meter bridge power, or integrated energy controls, Generac can turn those needs into revenue through gensets, systems integration, and controls products. That path is equipment exposure first, not long-duration primary-generation ownership.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Local issuer-primary captures place parts of Generac's new product and integrated energy-solutions offering into hyperscale / colo or similar data-center use cases.
  • The local investor-material capture is enough to establish platform capability in backup power and behind-the-meter energy systems, not a theme-only mapping.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Company materials position Generac as a supplier for data-center backup, microgrid, or behind-the-meter needs.
  • The company frames data-center-related demand as one direction for product and solutions expansion.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• GNRC fits best as Phase 5 E7 context because it helps separate backup-equipment exposure from purer onsite-generation exposure.
  • It has a real data-center power linkage, but it reads more like an extension of an industrial / commercial backup platform than an AI pure play.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The page does not have named repeatable data-center deployment evidence or AI-only revenue proof.
  • The page does not isolate data-center-only backlog, bookings, or segment economics.
  • The page also does not prove that data-center demand is large enough to dominate the overall platform outcome.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If future issuer-primary or filing evidence stops connecting Generac products to hyperscale, colo, or data-center backup use cases, this page's role should be downgraded.
  • If the data-center narrative remains only product marketing and fails to generate repeat deployment, revenue, or backlog evidence, the AI-to-revenue logic should be rewritten.
  • If the evidence resolves into generic commercial backup demand rather than data-center exposure, this page should leave Phase 5 E7 mainline tracking.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: Context / Needs-source. Proof gates: 1. Issuer-primary or filing evidence for named deployment, customer, or contract scope. 2. Repeatable data-center revenue, backlog, or booking evidence. 3. Clear proof that the data-center business is more than a marketing extension and materially contributes to the platform.

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Alphabet turns deployed compute into platform and application consumption across Google Cloud, Gemini, Workspace, and Search. The key issue is not broad Alphabet or broad Cloud totals but whether AI keeps driving higher-quality enterprise and consumer usage, subscriptions, and cloud consumption.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text:
• Lane: E9 AI Application Production and Data Lifecycle cloud / AI platform / application consumption owner, with a secondary demand-side link to Cloud and Compute Demand.
  • Boundary: Google Cloud, Gemini, Workspace, and Search convert deployed compute into enterprise and consumer usage. TPU and the model stack are secondary enablers, so GOOG does not absorb E2 compute-silicon ownership, E6 systems ownership, or any E7/E8 power and facility ownership.
  • Distinction: GOOG's advantage is GCP plus consumer distribution plus the search feedback loop, not physical-chain ownership.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text:
• Enterprise purchases of GCP AI infrastructure, AI solutions, and Workspace / Gemini related services convert into consumption fees, subscriptions, and contract revenue.
  • Consumer AI usage in Search and Gemini can monetize through query activity, ad effectiveness, subscriptions, and retention.
  • Broad Alphabet revenue, broad Google Cloud revenue, and Search growth are still not the same as direct AI revenue.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Q1 FY2026 consolidated revenue was USD 109.9B, up 22%.
  • Google Search and other revenue was USD 60.399B, up 19%.
  • Google Cloud revenue was USD 20.0B, up 63%; Cloud operating income was USD 6.598B.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Cloud backlog exceeded USD 460B, and the company said it nearly doubled quarter over quarter.
  • Gemini Enterprise paid monthly active users grew 40% quarter over quarter.
  • First-party models handled more than 16B tokens per minute through direct API use.
  • The Trillium TPU capture shows Google continuing to use TPU as part of its own AI training and serving stack.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• First-party models, TPU, Cloud, and Search distribution may create a cost, data, and distribution loop that benefits both enterprise AI spend and consumer application usage.
  • In this wiki, TPU remains a secondary platform-enabler role and does not absorb E2 compute-silicon ownership.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• Google Cloud revenue is not directly equivalent to AI revenue.
  • Search growth is not wholly AI, and backlog is not wholly AI or guaranteed to retain current margin.
  • TPU roadmap and product existence do not make GOOG an E2 compute-silicon or E6 systems owner in this wiki.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• AI experiences increase usage but weaken ad clicks, pricing, or query economics.
  • Cloud growth/backlog conversion slows while data-center investment and depreciation rise.
  • Enterprise AI workloads do enter GCP, but profit and retention fail to cover the higher capex burden.
  • Antitrust remedies restrict default access, ad technology, or distribution.

docs.title: GS — Goldman Sachs
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-07-13 CEST

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text:
• Structural status: context
  • Current role: Market-found
  • Primary lane: Phase 5 E10 cross-theme portfolio; capital-markets / investment-bank benchmark
  • Boundary: GS's durable role is the benchmark for investment banking, market making, financing, and institutional wealth distribution; it is not a standalone AI revenue name and it does not absorb universal-bank, payments, consumer-credit, application-owner, or physical-infrastructure-owner roles
  • Action pointer: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: In the local issuer packet, GS is defined as a capital-markets platform with two pillars: Global Banking & Markets and Asset & Wealth Management. Its place in E10 is not that it belongs to the AI / data-center supply chain, but that it lets the wiki observe how AI capex, risk appetite, and sponsor activity flow into underwriting, M&A, trading, financing, and wealth allocation.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: For GS, AI is not a separate product line; it is more likely to appear first in client activity and internal productivity. If AI capex, M&A, refinancing, risk management, and wealth or alternatives allocation demand increase, GS can monetize that through advisory, underwriting, financing, market making, and AWM. The company also explicitly describes One Goldman Sachs 3.0 as an AI-propelled operating-model upgrade, but that is an efficiency bridge rather than a separate AI revenue bucket.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• In 2025, net revenues were $58.3 billion, earnings per share were $51.32, and ROE was 15.0%.
  • The company explicitly anchors strategy in Global Banking & Markets and Asset & Wealth Management; AWM had $3.6 trillion of assets under supervision and wealth-management client assets of $1.9 trillion.
  • The local IR packet shows first-quarter 2026 earnings per share of $17.55 and annualized ROE of 19.8%.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Management said 2026 could benefit from stronger strategic activity, FICC / Equities client flows, AWM growth opportunities, AI capital investment, and a more balanced regulatory environment.
  • One Goldman Sachs 3.0 is described as an AI-propelled operating model intended to unlock productivity gains and improve speed, agility, efficiency, and resilience.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• If AI drives more capital formation, hedging, structured financing, wealth allocation, and private-markets demand, GS should benefit through its existing capital-markets / investment-bank machine.
  • Those benefits should be read first as operating leverage inside existing franchises, not as a new standalone AI business segment.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The company has established a separately disclosed AI revenue bucket.
  • Broad firmwide actuals are enough to prove an independent AI contribution to revenue or profits.
  • GS should absorb the roles of universal banks, alternative-asset managers, payment networks, or application / infrastructure owners.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If later local issuer / SEC packets show that capital-markets activity is not converting into steadier reported earnings, the E10 role should remain benchmark-only rather than being promoted.
  • If the page turns One Goldman Sachs 3.0 into AI revenue proof, it is confusing internal productivity with external monetization.
  • If the role drifts into universal-bank ownership, private-markets ownership, payments, or physical-buildout ownership, the boundary is wrong.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: Context / Market-found investment-bank and capital-markets benchmark. E10 keeps only the cross-theme market-activity role; current action lives in Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger.

docs.text: Role: E10 cross-theme retail-brokerage, crypto, and financial-entry owner Structural status: active Formal discovery state: Market-found Updated: 2026-07-13; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Robinhood combines retail brokerage, crypto, subscriptions, and adjacent cash, card, and advisory services in one consumer financial entry point. Core revenue still comes from transactions, subscriptions, and broader financial-services usage rather than a standalone AI revenue line.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: HOOD belongs to the E10 cross-theme fintech portfolio, not an AI or data-center supply spine. It owns retail brokerage, crypto, and the consumer financial entry point. It does not absorb SOFI's digital-bank and lending platform, AFRM's BNPL merchant network, or a generic application or infrastructure-owner role.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: Cortex Digests and Cortex Assistant currently sit in the in-app insight, education, and service-experience layer. If they improve engagement, retention, Gold adoption, or transaction and asset usage, value still appears through existing subscription and financial-entry economics. AI is not separately disclosed as revenue.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Official IR materials, the about page, and the Q1 FY2026 8-K frame Robinhood as a broader financial-services entry point for a new generation of investors.
  • The Q1 FY2026 packet records 4.3 million Robinhood Gold subscribers and USD 50 million in Gold subscription revenue. Those are subscription actuals, not AI-attributed revenue.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• The company says Cortex Digests has been used by nearly 1 million customers and describes Cortex Assistant as an AI-powered insights tool still rolling out.
  • Those statements prove product deployment and usage, not standalone AI monetization.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• If Cortex improves research, education, and service experience, it may increase engagement, retention, and Gold value.
  • The result must be verified in paid, asset-retention, or usage outcomes rather than inferred from rollout alone.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• Cortex has created separable revenue or profit contribution.
  • Broad transaction, crypto, subscription, or asset growth is directly attributable to AI.
  • HOOD should absorb SOFI, AFRM, or a wider application or infrastructure role.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• Lower trading and crypto activity would directly weaken transaction-driven economics.
  • If Gold growth does not produce steadier retention and unit economics, subscription support weakens.
  • If Cortex continues to show only usage or rollout claims without paid or retention outcomes, AI remains an experience layer.

docs.title: HPS.A — Hammond Power Solutions
docs.text:
Updated: 2026-07-13

Industry page: Facility Electrical, Rack Power, Cooling, and Delivery

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: HPS.A is an Active / Market-found transformer / power-quality company with the body-only modifier former-half-hidden. It sits in the medium- and low-voltage distribution layer between the site electrical boundary and the energized rack. It benefits from data-center expansion and custom electrical demand, but it does not own E7 generation, E2 compute silicon, or E6 full systems.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text:
HPS.A's core products are dry-type transformers, power-quality products, and custom-engineered electrical solutions. The position is after power enters the site or building and before power reaches rack-level electrical equipment.

Its boundaries need to stay explicit: - It does not own E7 generation / grid / time-to-power assets and should not be reframed as a generation or utility-power name. - It does not own E2 compute silicon, so GPU or ASIC demand cannot be treated as HPS.A revenue by default. - It does not own E6 systems integration, so full rack, server, or site delivery should not be assigned to HPS.A.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text:
AI data-center expansion increases demand for internal distribution, voltage transformation, harmonic mitigation, and custom electrical content. HPS.A monetizes that through dry-type transformers, power-quality equipment, and custom-engineered distribution content rather than through AI software or server branding.

That mechanism still has to stay under issuer-claim discipline: the company has explicitly linked data-center expansion to custom-product demand, but it has not disclosed named hyperscalers, an AI revenue split, or a data-center backlog percentage.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• In its annual report, HPS.A defines itself as a supplier of dry-type transformers and power-quality solutions serving North American electrical and industrial end markets.
  • FY2025 results materials show record sales, backlog growth, and expansion in private-label / custom-engineered solutions.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• The official Data Centers page targets data centers as an explicit vertical with relevant product and solution positioning; that is company positioning, not customer-purchase or revenue proof.
  • Management links part of the growth to datacentre expansion and demand for custom-engineered solutions.
  • Company framing supports the idea that HPS.A supplies customized transformer and distribution-related content for data-center deployments.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• If AI campuses keep expanding, medium- and low-voltage distribution plus power-quality demand inside the site should rise with them, creating more opportunity for HPS.A's custom electrical content.
  • HPS.A monetizes longer-cycle project electrical content rather than the faster and more direct power ramps seen in GPU or rack-PSU names.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• It is not yet proven that HPS.A has attributable revenue from a named hyperscaler or AI campus deployment.
  • It is not yet proven how much of backlog can be cleanly split into data-center or AI-related orders.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If later issuer-primary materials stop linking data-center expansion to custom-engineered growth, this page should be downgraded.
  • If revenue becomes mainly a broad industrial or commercial cycle story again and data centers fall back to a minor footnote, the core framing should shrink.
  • If new evidence shows HPS.A's role in data centers is mostly generic replacement content rather than specification-driven electrical infrastructure, the page needs to be rewritten.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text:
Active / Market-found; modifier: former-half-hidden. The E8 role is transformer / power quality from the site electrical boundary to the energized rack, with a hard boundary at not owning E7 generation, E2 compute silicon, or E6 systems.

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Hubbell is the E8 electrical equipment and connectivity platform from the grid toward the site boundary, turning grid-to-site connection, protection, and electrical attachment into a usable site-entry condition.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: HUBB's primary lane is electrical and utility equipment plus connectivity context: transmission and distribution components, substation-related hardware, connectors, protection, grounding, communications, and site-entry electrical accessories. It is an equipment owner, not an EPC contractor; it does not own rack-side UPS or thermal infrastructure, and it does not own upstream generation and fuel assets or server and networking-system manufacturing.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: An AI campus first needs power that can be connected, protected, and handed into the site before in-building distribution and rack energization matter. Load-center expansion raises the amount and specification of utility, substation, site-entry, and datacenter electrical products, and Hubbell monetizes that grid-to-site electrical content.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• The FY2025 10-K and the Q1 2026 10-Q and earnings call show HUBB spanning Utility Solutions and Electrical Solutions across utility-side and site-side electrical hardware.
  • In Q1 2026 management explicitly discussed growth tied to data center and Grid Infrastructure demand, with hyperscaler, colocation, transmission, and substation demand inside the current business context.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Management frames datacenter demand, grid modernization, load growth, and the 765kV transmission opportunity as important future demand sources.
  • The May 2026 NSI 8-K, press release, and term-loan 8-K establish that Hubbell signed and arranged financing for the transaction; if it closes, NSI's electrical fittings, connectors, wire-management, and related datacenter and network-infrastructure products would extend Electrical Solutions.
  • The NSI deal framing stresses complementarity with Electrical Solutions and names datacenter and network infrastructure as strategic verticals; that is issuer growth framing, not a disclosed AI revenue breakout.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• If hyperscaler and colocation campuses expand and require more site-entry electrical work, a platform like Hubbell should benefit from higher electrical content per site even without owning downstream rack power.
  • HUBB's durable E8 anchor value is that it keeps ownership of the "can power safely enter the site and connect reliably into the facility" layer, rather than collapsing that ownership into EPC execution or rack thermal systems.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The current local evidence does not isolate AI revenue for HUBB, and it does not prove that datacenter-related electrical growth will durably outgrow the broader utility and electrical base business.
  • The current local evidence does not support HUBB owning utility interconnection EPC, substation construction execution, or rack and facility thermal infrastructure; those remain separate owners.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If later disclosure shows datacenter electrical demand was only a short-lived order spike without sustained content or attach, the E8 anchor thesis weakens.
  • If NSI integration reduces execution quality or fails to deepen datacenter and site-entry content, the current boundary call should be revisited.
  • If the page starts treating HUBB as an EPC contractor, a time-to-power asset owner, or a rack-thermal owner without local-source support, that is a kill signal.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: Role: Core / Market-found. Stable E8 owner for grid-to-site electrical equipment and connectivity context; not an E7 generation/fuel owner and not an E6 server or networking-system manufacturer.

docs.title: INTC — Intel
docs.text: Role: spine 2 x86 CPU/host-compute context; foundry is a secondary spine 5 role Structural status: context Formal discovery state: Bridge / Benchmark Evidence through: 2026-04-23; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Intel earns from client/server CPUs and platform products while operating a capital-intensive foundry. Its direct compute mechanism is host CPU and DCAI demand. Foundry/advanced packaging is a separate manufacturing thesis with different economics and cannot be used to blur product and factory execution.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: INTC's primary context is the x86 CPU/host node in Semiconductors and Foundational Compute. Intel Foundry and advanced packaging secondary-link Semiconductor Manufacturing, Advanced Packaging, Test, and Materials; manufacturing revenue, internal transfers, and external-customer proof require separate analysis.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: AI servers and agentic inference can increase host CPU, I/O, and platform demand, becoming DCAI product revenue. Foundry must earn wafer/package revenue through yield, volume, customer commitments, utilization, and capex returns; CPU growth is not foundry proof.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Q1 2026 revenue was USD 13.6B, up 7%; DCAI revenue was USD 5.1B, up 22%.
  • GAAP gross margin was 39.4% and GAAP operating margin (23.1)%; non-GAAP operating margin was 12.3%.
  • Quarterly cash from operations was USD 1.1B, leaving material profitability/cash constraints.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text: Management says inference/agentic AI raises CPU, wafer, and advanced-packaging demand and stresses factory-network supply. External foundry customers, volume, and returns remain incomplete.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text: AI systems still require host CPUs, so Intel can benefit from CPU refresh and platform attach even if accelerators capture most value.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text: DCAI growth does not prove foundry success. Product improvement does not prove external foundry share, yield, or ROIC, and manufacturing capex is not AI revenue.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• DCAI share/revenue slows and server CPU competitiveness fades.
  • Foundry yield, external customers, or utilization do not improve while capex consumes cash.
  • GAAP/non-GAAP gaps, restructuring, or asset burdens expand persistently.
  • Product and manufacturing roadmaps are delayed together.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: INTC is Context / Bridge / Benchmark: CPU is compute context and foundry is a secondary spine 5 thesis.

docs.title: JCI — Johnson Controls
docs.text: Role: Phase 5 E8 spine 8 site electrical boundary to energized rack; JCI is the cooling / building-controls benchmark with an explicit proof gate Structural status: context Formal discovery state: Bridge / Benchmark Evidence through: 2026-04-21; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Johnson Controls is a building cooling, controls, and data-center-solutions platform, not a pure AI cooling winner. In E8 it serves as the cooling / building-controls benchmark, but any hidden framing must clear a stricter source gate first.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: JCI sits after the site electrical boundary and around the operating room layer: Applied HVAC, Silent-Aire, YORK, thermal management, building automation and controls, security, and fire protection. It does not own upstream generation / fuel, and it does not own E6 servers / network systems. It sells the thermal / controls stack at the building and data-hall layer.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: As AI data-center power density and uptime requirements rise, cooling, high-density thermal management, controls, monitoring, fire protection, and security all scale with it. JCI monetizes that through data-center solutions, Applied HVAC, modular data-center cooling, building controls, and related services, not through servers or network equipment themselves.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• The official release, 10-Q, and earnings slides jointly support the conclusion that Americas orders and backlog growth were primarily driven by data-center projects.
  • The 10-Q explicitly says Americas organic growth was led by Applied HVAC and Controls.
  • The 10-Q describes Johnson Controls as a platform around energy efficiency, decarbonization, thermal management, and mission-critical performance, explicitly naming data centers as one of the rapidly expanding industries it serves.
  • The data-center and thermal-management product pages show a real current solutions stack across YORK, Silent-Aire, thermal management, building controls, security, and fire protection.
  • The data-center page describes Silent-Aire as a data-center-solutions leader focused on Modular Data Centers, CRAC, and CRAHU systems.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• The company positions itself as a dedicated global data-center solutions partner and emphasizes hundreds of successful data-center projects, global scalability, and engineered consistency.
  • Management raised FY26 guidance in the Q1 results materials, but that guidance should not be treated as a direct AI-cooling attribution.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• JCI is a broad cooling / building-controls benchmark rather than a pure-play AI cooling name because monetization is spread across HVAC, thermal management, controls, safety, and services.
  • Data-center project momentum is real, but it is better read as a repricing entry point for a building-systems platform than as a fully closed hidden-name thesis.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The current raw packet does not provide clean data-center revenue share, standalone high-density-cooling revenue or margin, or clearer named-customer / attach-rate proof.
  • needs-source-before-any-hidden-gate must remain in force: without cleaner source-backed revenue mix or project monetization proof, JCI should not be upgraded into a hidden-thesis conclusion.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If later materials stop supporting the claim that Americas orders / backlog are primarily data-center-driven, JCI's data-center read-through should be downgraded.
  • If the cooling / controls / safety stack remains broad but still lacks measurable revenue or margin proof, the benchmark role should not be upgraded.
  • If broader building exposure dilutes the data-center increment, or competition compresses thermal-management project margins, JCI should remain bridge / benchmark only.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: JCI's current role is Context/benchmark; its formal state is Bridge / Benchmark. needs-source-before-any-hidden-gate remains only a workflow modifier, meaning any hidden framing requires harder source-backed monetization proof first.

docs.title: JPM — JPMorgan Chase
docs.text: Last updated: 2026-07-13 CEST

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text:
• Structural status: context
  • Current role: Market-found
  • Primary lane: Phase 5 E10 cross-theme portfolio; universal-bank benchmark
  • Boundary: JPM's durable role is the large universal-bank base that shows how deposits, lending, payments, custody, investment banking, and wealth distribution absorb corporate and market activity; it is not a standalone AI revenue name and it does not absorb payment-network, fintech, consumer-credit, application-owner, or physical-infrastructure-owner roles
  • Action pointer: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: In the local issuer packet, JPM appears as a large universal-bank platform spanning Consumer & Community Banking, Commercial & Investment Bank, and Asset & Wealth Management, with dedicated technology and quarterly-disclosure entry points. Its E10 value is as a benchmark for how macro conditions and AI-capex spillover reach the large-bank base, not as part of any AI / data-center supply spine.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: For JPM, AI is at most an indirect bridge, not a standalone revenue bucket. If AI capex and enterprise expansion create more financing, trading, payments, treasury, custody, and wealth-allocation activity, JPM can earn more through its existing universal-bank and investment-banking engines via fees, net interest income, and asset-management-related revenue; technology may also improve internal efficiency. But the current local issuer sources do not disclose AI as a separate revenue line, so broad bank-level actuals cannot be written up as AI monetization proof.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• The local IR packet explicitly lists Consumer & Community Banking, Commercial & Investment Bank, and Asset & Wealth Management as core platforms.
  • The company maintains a separate quarterly-earnings hub; the current packet does not break AI out as a reporting line.
  • The current local sources do not disclose a standalone AI revenue bucket.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Technology is an explicit capability area in official IR navigation, showing that the company treats technology and operations as part of its operating infrastructure.
  • The quarterly-earnings page is the formal management channel for actual results and forward-looking commentary, but the current local packet does not break AI out as a reporting segment.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• If AI increases corporate treasury, capital raising, market making, payments, custody, and wealth-allocation activity, JPM should benefit through its existing universal-bank machine.
  • That benefit is better understood as spillover from client activity and internal efficiency than as a new AI product revenue bucket.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• AI has become a separately trackable revenue or profit disclosure.
  • AI-related client activity is already large enough to dominate the bank's earnings profile.
  • JPM should absorb the roles of V — Visa, SOFI — SoFi Technologies, AFRM — Affirm Holdings, or any infrastructure owner.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If later local issuer / SEC packets show that this page is missing more specific bank-segment or quarter-actual disclosure, raw evidence should be refreshed before the judgment is strengthened.
  • If the page drifts back into treating broad bank earnings as AI revenue proof, it should revert to the stricter indirect-bridge framing.
  • If the role drifts into payment-network, fintech, consumer-credit, or data-center asset ownership, the boundary is wrong.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: Context / Market-found universal-bank benchmark. E10 keeps only the cross-theme financial-base role; current action lives in Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger.

docs.title: KLAR — Klarna Group
docs.text: Role: E10 cross-theme portfolio prose; BNPL, digital-bank, and merchant-consumer network owner Structural status: active Formal discovery state: Market-found Evidence as of: 2026-07-13; action SOT: Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text: Klarna's stable position is a merchant-consumer network that ties together BNPL, merchant payments, consumer entry points, and digital-bank relationships. This is first a consumer-finance network and user-relationship owner, not B2B credit-decisioning infrastructure and not an ecommerce platform or broader application / infrastructure owner.

docs.title: Lane and boundary
docs.text: KLAR sits on the fintech / consumer-credit side of E10 cross-theme portfolio prose. Its stable ownership is BNPL, digital-bank, and merchant-consumer network. It does not absorb UPST's AI/ML lending marketplace, PGY's B2B credit-decisioning / securitization infrastructure, or PDD's commerce / application-owner role.

docs.title: How AI becomes revenue
docs.text: Klarna's AI relevance shows up more in risk control, personalization, service automation, and merchant / consumer matching efficiency, but those all serve BNPL and network economics. Revenue first comes from payments, merchant relationships, and consumer-finance relationships, not a separable AI revenue line. Funding, credit, merchant, or GMV metrics do not automatically equal AI proof.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
• Local issuer source positions Klarna as a global digital bank and flexible-payments provider.
  • The FY2025 and Q1 FY2026 results pages provide issuer-primary operating actuals supporting the view that this is a BNPL / merchant-consumer network rather than a single-product tool.

docs.title: Issuer claim
docs.text:
• Issuer framing consistently emphasizes flexible payments, merchant reach, consumer relationships, and digital-bank positioning.
  • That framing proves network and product positioning, but it does not by itself prove AI as a separate revenue line.

docs.title: Reasonable inference
docs.text:
• If user retention, merchant adoption, and credit control stay balanced, Klarna's network economics can continue improving.
  • That improvement belongs to BNPL and digital-bank network execution, not to B2B underwriting infrastructure or ecommerce-platform ownership.

docs.title: Not proven
docs.text:
• The current local source set does not isolate AI revenue.
  • Funding, credit loss, merchant growth, or GMV totals are not automatic proof of AI monetization.

docs.title: Value capture and boundary of misread
docs.text: Klarna captures value by combining consumer entry points, payment scenarios, merchant distribution, and bank-like account relationships into a high-frequency network. The misread boundary is turning it into B2B credit infrastructure, a pure lending marketplace, or rewriting merchant / consumer growth directly as AI monetization. KLAR owns the BNPL / digital-bank / merchant-consumer network role here.

docs.title: Risks and kill criteria
docs.text:
• If credit losses, funding costs, or regulation damage network economics, margin room contracts first.
  • If merchant adoption and consumer activity fall out of balance, the network effect weakens.
  • If later local issuer / SEC evidence still consists only of broad consumer-finance totals without more specific automation or attach proof, this page should stay restrained on AI-relevance language.

docs.title: Current role
docs.text: KLAR is Active / Market-found. Its stable ownership is BNPL, digital-bank, and merchant-consumer network. It does not absorb the owner boundaries of UPST, PGY, or PDD. Any current action lives only in Tech Mainline Research Unified Ticker Ledger.

docs.text: Centrus is an upstream uranium-enrichment and nuclear-fuel supplier, especially around HALEU capability. In this wiki it represents advanced-nuclear fuel supply, not data-center onsite power, facility electrical work, or cooling delivery.
